name: Grand Theft Auto IV: Complete Edition
review:
I never had the privilege to experience this game at launch in 2008. My first real Grand Theft Auto I've ever owned without playing over at someone else's house was the next installment released in 2013.

I gotta say, playing all 3 campaigns from start to finish definitely holds a candle to the franchise in general.
Liberty City as a map may not be as big as Los Santos or Vice City, but it sure does make you feel small in the grand scheme of everything. It holds a mirror to each protagonist and shows them what will happen to them, just about the same as Red Dead Redemption 1 and 2.

Everything connects so well in both main game and DLC content. The game never holds back any punches when it comes to Niko, Johnny and Luis' struggles surviving in Liberty City. The deuteragonists also play an important part in their stories as well, and they don't overstay their welcome.

Despite all of the problems that Rockstar/T2 have put forth in the recent years, I highly recommend picking this up as soon as you can. You may have to install some restoration mods in order to have the launch experience via Fusion Fix, Console Foliage, Radio Restoration; the list goes on.

One can only hope that Grand Theft Auto VI will have just about the same kind of grit and power this game has. It may be flashy from all of the trailers, but time will only tell.

name: Grand Theft Auto IV: Complete Edition
review:
Ahoy, Swoonds here.
Today I’m reviewing a game so gritty, so cold, so full of immigrant depression and high-speed vehicular manslaughter that OSHA banned it in three states.
It’s Grand Theft Auto IV — or as I like to call it: Slavic Guilt Simulator 2008.

"I came to America to forget the war. Turns out the war came too."
— Niko Bellic, War Criminal & Taxi Driver

This isn’t your sunshine and Ferraris GTA. This isn’t pimpin’ hoes in San Andreas or flying motorcycles in GTA Online while being hunted by a 13-year-old with mommy’s credit card and a suppressed KD ratio.
No. This is GTA IV.
A game about coming to the land of dreams, only to be smacked in the face with reality, bills, and your cousin’s pathological gambling addiction.

You play as Niko Bellic, an Eastern European ex-soldier, ex-hitman, and current regret-fueled meat sack. Niko immigrates to Liberty City to escape his past, but quickly learns that past, present, and future are just synonyms for "things that will go horribly wrong."

"Roman, I’ve been in America five minutes and I’ve already committed 17 felonies."
— Niko, before the tutorial ends

STORY
The story of GTA IV is less about gangsters and more about the weight of sin.
Niko doesn’t want revenge — he needs it, like some people need therapy or a functioning liver.
Everyone you meet is either:

A scumbag

An opportunist

A liar

Or your cousin Roman

You climb the criminal ladder while wrestling with PTSD, betrayal, and trying not to throttle Roman every time he calls you to "go bowling."

GTA IV is bleak, but it’s good bleak.
Like a Serbian version of Breaking Bad, if Walt drove a stolen cab and snorted vodka off a tire iron.

"I killed people. Smuggled people. Sold people. And you say I should apologize for that? If I was sorry, it wouldn’t mean anything."
— Niko, during his TED Talk on moral ambiguity

WORLD
Liberty City in GTA IV is alive.
Not in a Ubisoft open world checklist kind of way, but in the holy shit I just watched a guy get hit by a car and sue the driver while yelling in Spanish kind of way.

The game doesn’t give you the biggest map. It gives you the densest, most realistic urban hellscape ever crafted in pixels.
You don’t explore Liberty City — you survive it.
Rain-soaked streets. Sirens echoing in the distance. Bums shouting about lizard people. This place is New York, distilled through a cracked bottle of vodka and a suicide note.

"The American Dream is a lie, cousin. It is a lie told to children and foreign men with good aim."
— Niko, 5 minutes before reenacting the Yugoslav Wars in Broker

GAMEPLAY
Shooting? Serviceable.
Cover system? Exists.
Driving? Like piloting a wet brick through an ice rink while being shot at by Albanian gangsters.

But here’s the thing: that’s the point.
You’re not supposed to feel powerful.
You're supposed to feel like a wounded pit bull, barely holding it together — because that’s what Niko is.

And when it clicks?
You become the storm.
Every firefight is personal. Every death — intimate. Every mission — another chance to make wrong decisions for the right reasons.

CHARACTERS
Roman: A walking scam email with a gambling problem. Will die or survive based on how much bowling you do.

Brucie: Human cocaine. Has never had a real thought in his life.

Little Jacob: The only man alive who can fire an Uzi and quote Marcus Garvey mid-fight.

Pegorino: Italian mobster. Diet Tony Soprano. Still better than The Sopranos ending.

Dwayne: The saddest man in gaming. Killing him should be a war crime.

Playboy X: Human betrayal in a leather jacket.

Also, half the cops are voiced by comedians, and one of them literally says, “I joined the force to steal from evidence lockers.”

THEMES
GTA IV is about violence, yes.
But more than that — it’s about the cost.
About escaping your past only to find it waiting in a back alley with a crowbar.

It’s about chasing money, power, and peace — and realizing you can only ever afford one.

It’s about freedom — and how freedom in Liberty City comes with a price tag and usually ends in a shallow grave.

"In this country, they expect you to pretend to care. I am through pretending."
— Niko, delivering the most Slav line since the invention of the squat

CONCLUSION
GTA IV is not for everyone.
It’s slow. It’s heavy. It’s cynical.
But it’s also genius.

This isn’t just one of the best Rockstar games ever made — it’s one of the best stories told in gaming.
It’s Shakespeare with an AK.
It’s Dostoyevsky in a tracksuit.
It’s the story of a man trying to build a new life — while every bridge he walks across collapses behind him.

If GTA V is about the American Dream, GTA IV is about waking up from it.

10/10
Would shoot Dardan in the balls again.

name: Last Epoch
review:
I really like this game, it's a great take on the ARPG genre. In many ways its much better than D4. The story is engaging enough for the campaign. The gear mechanics is different and IMO better and the skill system active/passive skill system is very meaningful gameplay wise; I looked forward to leveling to build my character. The gameplay feels good, the skills could have a more visceral feel but overall they are good and character defining. For the price I 100% recommend it as a very good ARPG that will give you several weeks of great fun.

What Last Epoch lacks is a reason to keep playing after hitting level 90ish. I think this an excellent game and I've been trying to think of why this is and here's what I think. 

The later tier skills (at least for the acolyte) are not very impactful on the build, just incrementally increasing defense or offense. I get that there shouldn't be a gameplay defining skill at level 100, or maybe there should be and level 100 is too high. Personally I gave up around level 95.

This leaves gear as the last venue of big jumps in char building and there's no NEW gear at high levels, just RNG for new gear with ability to improve it. For some gameplay defining pieces I really enjoy that, I enjoy that I had a piece early on that gave me a unique feel skill, but it also gets boring seeing the same pieces drop over and over and over especially when leveling up becomes very slow. I get thats how ARPGs are, but after a few weeks of nothing its boring. I can also say the level restriction on improving items in the Eternity Cache pissed me off so much I stopped playing for a few days. I think the process is complex enough, I just didn't see that there was a level restriction on items and when I couldn't add the affix after burning a key, doing the dungeon and beating the boss, it was very frustrating.

The Idol system for Acolytes is garbage. It's better for other classes, but the whole intended system about playing a char w low life and high ward to get high dmg, that's just not worth it in an ARPG. I couldn't find a guide that promoted that mechanic and overall most ppl avoid "glass canon builds" as in my experience it shows a lack of forethought in surviveability. As much as the devs have put into the Idol system with the Woven web dungeons, I simply use it to make sure I'm resist capped which gives me 1 or 2 large spots for mostly meh large idols (again, as an acolyte).

Which leads me to the last gripe I have: either the games damage is too bursty or there isn't enough feedback on being damaged. I get the screen flashing and the audio queue from the char, but 1hp dmg and 1000hp dmg feels the same. As far as dmg being too bursty, I have the Woven Flesh Armor that has "100% Critical Strike Avoidance" which I assume means I can't be crit hit. And somehow a Soul Tank can teleport on top of me for a 1 shot kill me with all resists capped, 1718HP and 500-800 ward. Most of the times when I die it is a surprise. I didn't see my life or ward being low seconds before.

I don't usually post to bitch, but I like this game I hope that the feedback I give is taken constructively.

I don't want to offend either the game's authors or its loyal fans. But the game looks cheap in all its aspects.
Graphics - nice, but poor. Poor detail, poor visualization of effects (in some places they are simply not there, like, for example, during teleportation, and you can't look at fire without tears), poor interactivity with world objects (I can't talk to NPCs without walking through them).
Music. I just turned it off.
Gameplay. There is no feeling of smashing crowds of monsters to pieces. Some just burst like bubbles, some - flop on the floor and disappear. Locations, as I understand it, are static, not generated. If so, then why is there a "fog of war"? I went through a location, it was all reflected on the map, came back - everything was again hidden by "fog". For what? And why am I returning via teleportation to a completely rebooted location?
Leveling up is quite interesting, reminds me of that in Grim Dawn. But I haven't seen what it's like in the endgame yet.
Crafting requires instructions (they're in the game). Otherwise, it's impossible to understand how to use it.

In general, if Steam had a "poor" rating, I would have given it that. Alas, here it only says "not recommended".

review:
I love this game.... right up until the end.

It scratches that "I want to use my brain for very specific things and mash buttons the rest of the time" itch, has a huge amount of variety in builds, and the unique items have some really creative options that entirely redefine a build and make you try out combos you hadnt considered before. 

But once you get to the monoliths, the game doesn't tell you the main storyline isn't finished yet (as of tombs season) - you get redirected into this area with false expectations on what you're intended to accomplish, and oh my god is it a _drag_. It's the same experience over and over and over and over again, with tiny little upgrades here and there but mostly the same useless unique gear over and over (and the game feels incredibly biased to giving you other classes gear - normally I'd chalk it up to the size of the random pool, but i consistently get the same mage/sentinel/rogue uniques and rarely get acolyte gear as an acolyte).

I can deal with this up to a point, that's the nature of the game, but when you reach corruption levels or end-state dungeons/arena, the enemies spike _massively_ and you're stuck with the same tiny or non-existent upgrades. 

Example, the temporal dungeon - i can crush that on the second to last level with no issue. Last level? I get one shot for _EIGHT TIMES_ my health. By a random projectile. When I'm using gear that specifically removes evade in favor of CC.

name: Last Epoch
review:
In a post-Diablo IV, post-Path of Exile 2 world, Last Epoch still manages to carve out a firm place in the ARPG pantheon—not by reinventing the genre, but by polishing it to a brilliant, time-twisting shine.

Blending fast-paced combat, deep character customization, and an engaging time-travel narrative, Last Epoch has matured into a highly addictive action RPG that rewards both hardcore theorycrafters and casual dungeon-crawlers alike.

Set in the fractured world of Eterra, Last Epoch weaves a surprisingly competent time-travel narrative into its hack-and-slash loop. You’ll leap between different eras—ruined futures, ancient pasts, apocalyptic presents—fighting corrupted gods, temporal monsters, and undead horrors.

Each timeline feels distinct, not just visually but mechanically, affecting loot drops, enemy types, and progression. It’s more than a narrative gimmick—it’s a core design element that adds variety and replayability.

Combat in Last Epoch hits that sweet spot: meaty, fast, and visually rewarding, without being overloaded by animation spam or screen clutter.

Skills feel weighty. Enemies react with impact. And while the pace is closer to Diablo III than the ultra-fast chaos of Path of Exile, it still gets plenty intense during big mob pulls or monolith pushes.

Bosses—especially in the endgame—require attention to mechanics and positioning, avoiding the typical ARPG pitfall of “click and delete.”

Last Epoch features 5 base classes (Sentinel, Mage, Rogue, Acolyte, and Primalist), each branching into 3 specialized Mastery Classes, unlocking entirely unique skill paths. That’s 15 total subclasses, each with their own identity.

Every skill has its own talent tree, allowing you to deeply specialize. You don’t just slot a fireball—you can evolve it to home in, explode, freeze, or leech health. It makes builds feel truly custom-tailored, even at early levels.

Add in a robust passive tree, a loot-driven crafting system (more on that below), and you’ve got one of the most satisfying build systems in any ARPG.

Crafting in Last Epoch is one of its strongest and most accessible features. It strikes a rare balance: meaningful, powerful, but not overwhelming.

You use runes, glyphs, and shards to upgrade and modify gear, with a visible “fracture” chance that adds risk. It's transparent, tactile, and allows for endgame-worthy gear without pure RNG farming.

It feels like a system made for the player, not just for grind extension.

At endgame, Last Epoch offers several meaningful options:
-Monolith of Fate: A branching, customizable challenge system with rewards, modifiers, and evolving timelines.
-Dungeons: Procedural and narrative-driven, with unique bosses and loot.
-Arena: Horde-style challenge mode for leaderboard chasers.
-Cycles: Last Epoch’s take on seasonal content, offering fresh ladders, loot themes, and balance changes.

It’s not as brutally dense as PoE, but it’s more structured and flexible than Diablo IV’s endgame. In short: you get goals, variety, and progression without burnout.

Graphically, Last Epoch won’t rival AAA blockbusters, but it has come a long way since its early access days. Spell effects are crisp, environments are distinct, and performance is now solid and smooth, even during chaotic battles.

The UI is clean and functional, especially the inventory, skill planning, and crafting windows. Controller support is decent but still not perfect—keyboard and mouse are the clear best way to play.

After a long wait, Last Epoch’s online multiplayer launched in 2024, and it’s been a big win. You can now group up, trade (in limited formats), and take on Monoliths or dungeons together.

The devs at Eleventh Hour Games are highly engaged, the roadmap is transparent, and the community is genuinely one of the more helpful and theory-driven out there.

No pay-to-win. No loot boxes. Just solid design choices and respect for the player base.

While Last Epoch is excellent, it’s not flawless:
-Visual design can feel generic in some zones
-Story beats are decent, but not groundbreaking
-Loot filters require a learning curve to maximize quality-of-life
-Build meta can get stale between cycle updates

Still, these are polish-level gripes, not structural flaws.

Last Epoch is one of the most balanced, flexible, and rewarding ARPGs on the market today. It doesn’t try to out-bloat PoE or out-gloss Diablo, but instead focuses on clarity, customization, and satisfying combat.

It’s a game where your build is your creation, where loot matters, and where your time feels respected.

If you’ve been looking for a deep but approachable ARPG that respects your intelligence and time, this is the one.

Pros:
-Deep, flexible class and skill system
-Transparent and rewarding crafting
-Satisfying combat with strong build diversity
-Varied endgame that respects player agency
-Active devs, healthy updates, no P2W nonsense

Cons:
-Some zones lack visual distinction
-Loot filter setup can be overwhelming early on
-Story is serviceable, not epic
-Late-game content can get meta-dependent

Last Epoch isn’t about breaking the mold—it’s about perfecting the cast. A polished, addictive, and endlessly replayable ARPG that respects its genre and its players.

Rating: 8/10

name: Half-Life 2: Lost Coast
review:
Half-Life 2: Lost Coast is a nerd’s dream. I don’t even know where to start with this masterpiece because it’s so much more than just a game—it’s a second life. No, seriously. Half-Life 2: Lost Coast is the ultimate nerdy science fiction adventure, a massive sandbox filled with endless opportunities for exploration, creativity, and (of course) puzzle solving. And the best part? The sheer depth of the world, the lore, and the freedom to do absolutely anything you want. It’s a dream come true for any player who loves getting lost in a detailed, living, breathing universe.

The sheer freedom in how you can approach everything is insane. Want to be a sneaky scientist, lurking in the shadows, silently taking out your enemies one by one? You can do that. Want to take on a full-on tank build with armor and two massive guns, smashing through anything in your path? Also possible. Or maybe you’re more of the engineer type, solving environmental puzzles and making traps? Yeah, you can definitely do that too. The ability to specialize your character however you want, down to the perks, gives you a level of customization that I’ve never experienced before. Every time you level up, it feels like a mini Christmas, getting to choose between new abilities that completely alter how you tackle the world. You’ll feel like you’re unlocking new powers every time you hit that level-up screen.

Let’s talk about the lore. If you’re the type of player who gets obsessed with deep world-building and history, Half-Life 2: Lost Coast is a literal goldmine. Every broken down, abandoned building, every journal entry, every random NPC conversation… it’s all part of this vast narrative web that pulls you deeper and deeper into the story. I’ve spent hours just analyzing the environmental storytelling in the game, piecing together the histories of the various factions, the Combine, and the forgotten military outposts scattered across the map. It’s like every corner of Lost Coast has something new for you to discover, and each discovery feels rewarding. The best part? None of it is ever forced on you. You don’t have to read or engage in every little story, but if you do? You’re rewarded with this rich, immersive world that feels lived in.

Combat in Half-Life 2: Lost Coast is satisfying, and there are so many ways to approach it. Sure, you can spam shotguns and watch enemies explode into a fiery mess, but there’s a certain thrill in sneaking up behind an enemy and landing a perfect headshot with a pistol. Or, if you’re like me, you’ll spend hours perfecting your grenade throws, pulling off precise shots with the perfect weapon setup. There’s just something so fun about seeing enemies scattered across the environment after a well-timed shot. And don’t even get me started on physics puzzles—using the gravity gun to manipulate objects and create new paths? YES, PLEASE.

If you’re into modding, Half-Life 2: Lost Coast is the ultimate playground. I can’t even count how many times I’ve gone down a mod rabbit hole, tweaking everything from textures to adding new levels. The modding community for this game is insane, and the best part is how modders keep the game alive with new content years after its release. I’ve got mods that add new locations to explore, new enemies to fight, and even new ways to play. The flexibility in how you can customize the game makes every playthrough feel fresh and new, no matter how many times you’ve done it.

All in all, Half-Life 2: Lost Coast isn’t just a game—it’s a nerdy universe where the possibilities are endless. The world is rich, the lore is deep, and the freedom to create the character you want to be makes it one of the most immersive experiences out there. Sure, you could blast through the main story and be done in 30 hours, but if you’re like me, you’ll end up spending hundreds of hours just enjoying the little details, finding new locations, and perfecting your combat strategy. There’s truly no other game quite like it, and honestly, if you haven’t played it yet, what are you even doing with your life?

Almost all of the characters behave and sound like juvenile teenagers doing their impression of what they think to be cool. Including your character, V and Johnny (who you will hear plenty of). Especially jarring when juxtaposed against a dystopian world dealing with (even if superficially) heavy themes like hypercapitalism, oppression, hedonism, body horror etc. Almost nothing feels believable, sensible or consequential. 

Speaking of Johnny, Keanu Reeves' performance is awful. 

There are also still tons of graphical glitches like characters and cars clipping through the environment etc.

Got to Act 3 and put in a few hours in the DLC, but can't bring myself to finish. It'll be too soon if I hear another slang like 'preem', 'choom', 'sitch', 'delta' and 'gonk'.

name: Cyberpunk 2077
review:
The game has grown to be one-of-a-kind for many reasons. Graphics, obviously, becoming the new "can I run it?" game. Chances are that the answer is "Not at over 60fps without DLSS." In my experience, the game runs well and is optimised enough to run smoothly without crashes, stuttering, or sudden frame-rate drops.

The story is brilliant, easily the highlight of the game for me. It has a lot of replay value thanks to the well thought-out perk system, and the combat (or alternatives to direct combat) keep the whole experience fresh and fun.

It's one of those games that you can have a blast playing by taking it easy, running side quests, or 100% focusing on the main story. It's well-made to be open to player choices.

The character designs in appearance and personality are fleshed-out and well-invested in. You see where some people live, work, and where they like to regular. It feels like a lived-in world.

It's worth a go.

review: It's unfinished, and was released as such. Over the years, though, the patches and DLC have really flushed out the game. Core mechanics like using MaxDocs to get health have been changed. Before updates, I would say it's worth a try but can get really frustrating with all the bugs and crashes. I put many hours in when Cyberpunk was in it's more janky state. In 2025 with Phantom Liberty, I still experience bugs and crashes, but they aren't game breaking, and due to the autosave feature the crashes don't set me back too far. Overall I have a really fun time with Cyberpunk, and there are plenty of mods out there to explore as well. Calling Cyberpunk 2077 a "bad game" feels ignorant. What, it isn't fun to zero some gonks with a katana using a slow-mo body mod? Come on, choom. Pick up some iron and make some eddies by playing Cyberpunk today.

name: Cyberpunk 2077
review:
One of my favorite games of all time.

From the very first day — bugs and all — I loved Cyberpunk 2077.

The storyline is unforgettable, the quests feel deep and emotional, and the entire world of Night City is both tragic and beautiful in its own broken way.

The music? Phenomenal. The gameplay? Addictive. The atmosphere? Unlike anything else.

I’ve bought this game on more than one platform because it truly stole my heart.

If I had to say something negative, it’s only this: I wish there was more. The story felt short, and while the city is stunning, I sometimes wished it felt more alive, with more things to interact with.

Still, Cyberpunk 2077 is a masterpiece — flawed, yes, but beautiful. One of the most memorable gaming experiences I've ever had.

review:
"The Most Fun I've Had Screaming Since My Last Family Reunion"

Dead by Daylight is a game where you either escape a bloodthirsty killer… or become the bloodthirsty killer. You know, wholesome weekend vibes.

As a survivor, I’ve mastered the art of panic-running into walls and pretending to understand what a “skill check” is. My main talent is screaming IRL when the killer pops out of nowhere like a cursed jack-in-the-box. I once hid in a locker for 5 minutes. The killer never found me. I also missed my friends getting slaughtered. Worth it.

As a killer, I enjoy long walks through the cornfield, gently breathing behind survivors, and smacking people mid-vault like a horror movie hall monitor. Nothing brings people together like yelling “WHERE DID HE GO?!” at a Meg who vanished into the fog like a magician on Red Bull.

The graphics are spooky, the lore is deeper than my emotional issues, and the matchmaking is just unpredictable enough to keep your blood pressure interesting. Every match is a chaotic dance of murder, friendship, betrayal, and someone DCing the moment they hear a chainsaw.

10/10, would get teabagged by Dwight again.

review:
As a game once highly anticipated, has now left me deeply disappointed. Firstly, the game is plagued by numerous bugs that severely impact gameplay. Whether it's character movement stuttering or scene loading errors, these frequent issues disrupt the gaming process and prevent players from immersing themselves in the game world, completely undermining the enjoyment of the game.
Secondly, the unreasonable matchmaking system is extremely frustrating. There is no logical pattern in rank matching, with low-rank players often matched against high-rank or even red-tier players. This vast disparity in player skill levels disrupts game balance. In matches, the uneven skill levels of teammates often leave low-rank players powerless against strong opponents, resulting in a poor gaming experience. Particularly when matched with teammates from different regions, such as Indian players, their gameplay and awareness often lead to frustration, making one question the purpose of such a matchmaking system.
Furthermore, recent content updates have faced serious issues. The highly anticipated Itou Junji collaboration skins were suddenly blocked in the Chinese region upon official release, making many players feel discriminated against and triggering a wave of negative reviews. Players' enthusiasm and expectations were ruthlessly dashed, and the official response, citing technical reasons, was unconvincing.
Additionally, some maps in the game have issues prone to disconnections, such as Lao Yang's Sanatorium, which frequently causes game freezes, seriously affecting the game's smoothness and continuity.

Gameplay is fun and varied with the spells you have at your disposal. Puzzles are good. But there are too many of them and it gets quite repetitive.

There's quite a lot it attempted to do and I respect the ambition. Some systems could have been more polished, but now there's a lot to do for the sequel.

review:
[h1]Wasted opportunity that somehow managed to make the magic stick bang-bang somewhat interesting[/h1]

Having finished the HP + FB movie marathon, I decided to board the wizarding world choo-choo train — merely 20 years too late. Yes, I somehow managed to dodge it back in elementary school by spending way too many hours playing Wolfenstein: Enemy Territory. Admittingly, I tried some of the HP games in the past — and they were absolutely dreadful. Game mechanics? Sleep inducing. Story? Oh, same shit as the movies but with some lame orb collection.

Given the hype around this game, I decided to give it the benefit of the doubt — and boy, am I glad I did.

From the very get-go, it’s clear as day that this game is a labour of love by the developers. I’m talking about the incredible detail of the castle, which feels incredibly immersive with all the activities it offers. It made me feel like I missed out on something great by not boarding that choo-choo train way back. And most importantly, the combat system wasn’t dreadful. In fact, I couldn’t come up with a single improvement to it — which says a lot. So, in theory, everything should have been great.

Well, it wasn’t. And it's due to a single thing... a thing so important for a game of this genre: the story. Without the slightest clue, I created a Slytherin character called Isydora Slaughterin — my pinnacle statement of trying to become a tyrant who inflicts their will upon the measly students that can’t hold a candle to my A+ grades (stay with me here, I’m compensating for average grades and being an Average Joe). Funnily enough, Isidora is actually one of the protagonists in the game. One who started with a potentially interesting backstory... only for it to be reduced to a generic and uninspiring ending.

And that’s the greatest shame about this game — it tried to satisfy everyone while keeping an appropriate age rating. I kinda expected it to have a more mature, intriguing, and thrilling storyline that might set things up for a sequel — especially given the aging fandom, most of whom are hitting (or about to hit) their 30s.

Overall, I’d definitely recommend the game at a reduced price. If you’re a Potterhead, it’s a must. If you’re not, you might still want to step halfway into that wormhole. It’s just sad that you can’t get completely sucked in — because the writers wanted to play it safe.

name: VRChat
review: As a furry, being able to present myself using an anthro character in VR is very important to me. So far this is the only app (other than Anyland which is just too much going on to be useful) where I can create and upload an avatar that represents how I prefer to see myself. It's quite new, so the process of creating and uploading an avatar is still very complicated and buggy. Many people complain that they upload avatars and they can select them, but they never rez. There's also the thing where you have to map every individual part of your body that moves (including each individual finger) to your avatar in the Unity application before you can upload it. On another note, the things you can do in this VR space are fairly limited and static: There's never anything new, so the few demo worlds that are available are all you get, and it gets boring quickly. It's like the devs just arrived at a point where they went "okay this is enough content, we're done." At the moment there's no way to change the luminosity of other avatars, so you've got those people who will crank the luminosity to maximum on their models so they glare in your face like direct sunlight. You've also got people who will make gigantic room-filling avatars and stand there waving their arms around in groups of people. While this app is an excellent concept, I see the freedom people have with avatar creation being stifled quite a bit because the way it is now just isn't scalable; the potential for abusive avatars palpable. Basically imagine all the problems jerks cause inSecond Life, but now it's all around you in 3D space.

review: I just recently started playing around with this VR experience or collection of games, or interactive application, it is hard to define really, but it is awesome.  This is now my new go to application to show off just how cool VR can be.  Not only does the communication with other uses work almost flawlessly (if both have good headsets and a microphone) but the app itself is beautifullly constructed with multiple "Worlds" on can visit.  Some of these worlds offer pretty fun competive multiplayer games, like capture the flag or gold with either laser pistols or six shooters (depending on the game) other experiences are in sight and sound, like multiple movie theater spots (where you can use your Youtube to play the content you desire), presentations rooms, etc.  There is so much to explore and/or create it is awesome.  Just last night I visited a moon base, not only was it beautiful and peaceful, I was surprised to see I could leave the moonbase and walk around the moon, jump in simulated low gravity and explore!   The avatars are full body and you can choose from a number of pre-created forms as well as upload your own.  I was standing next to Wolverine (with claws and everything) yesterday.    Definite a must have for any VR user.

review:
This is the best application for virtual reality, hands down. I have been a member of VRchat for over two years, and the community is what makes this place so special. Each "room" in VRchat is a direct upload of a scene in Unity (software used to create most VR experiences). This makes it very easy for community members to upload new rooms and content. The developers of VRchat are also making the games they have (Capture the Flag, Battle Discs, etc) available in the SDK. This means over the next few months anyone can adapt these games and create new versions of them!

VRchat is a great way to gain exposure to Unity/development...but you can also just have fun and talk to others here. Other social VR apps don't even compare in that feeling of community you get when you log in. Our meetups are on Sundays, but since its public release there have been people logged in continuously. 

Come join our community, and see for yourself what makes this such a special place!

name: VRChat
review:
Absolutely love VRChat and it's openness to user-generated content. The IK system for the avatars works really well especially if you find an avatar with proportions similar to your own body.

Pros
Stays pretty active with between 20-50 people at almost any time of day (pretty good for vr multiplayer)
Devs and moderators are really active, helpful, and love to show off what VRChat can offer
A few good CTF style games to play and Tron discs
Open to user-generated rooms so there could be more really fun stuff coming out soon
Easy to grab people from the hub and have them join you in a game
Easy to see what people are already playing or hanging out in
Its totally free
There are rooms where you can hang out and watch youtube videos with people
If a room is full, you can easily create a new instance of that room for new people to join

Cons
You need a pretty good understanding of Unity to create your own content (devs/community are making tutorials though)
Can sometimes be buggy/drop frames but not too often
Not as popular/active as Rec Room
There arent currently a ton of fun games
No user market place or workshop so you can easily download new avatars/etc (i think devs are considering it currently)

All things considered, VRChat is pretty dang amazing and a good spot to hang out and chat with people or play some fun games.

review:
I am having a VR setup since December and I have seen A LOT, that includes a ton of games, "experiences", demos. And also a bunch of social VR apps, incl. Altxxxxx, HiFi and some others. This one I have to say blows ALL these experiences out of the water - by miles!

Let me see. Today, this Friday night...I have been in a giant show which was excellently done with anime dancers. I climbed about a mile up in the sky with some people and then we dropped down. I have been in some sort of anime/game forest. I have been in a bowling alley which appeared very real, complete with 50s music and disco light :) I have been in a bar with about 20 people and a bar tender busy running around and serving drinks. I have been in an abandoned prison with scary ghosts, traps and all kinds of stuff. We have played games like CTF and we've been in an old Western town where we were the Sherrifs and shot some bad Bandit dudes :)

A lot of fun also with people showing off their insanely creative avatars. I took my headset off later on and realized that I "experienced" more things in one single night than a normal person could ever experience in "real life" in a night, uh..a week or a month even. This is just frickin' awesome beyond words.

From a technical point of view, the avatars are excellent and VRchat even allows making and importing your own from Unity. Lip sync, eye tracking and all. Some of the best avatars I have ever seen. The entire system seems polished and runs smooth.

VRChat must have hundreds of "worlds" including games etc. to choose from since you can browse them for an half an hour and still didn't see them all. This is crazy. Uh, that being said people can also design their own worlds and games and put them in there. Possibilites: Endless. MIND. BLOWN.

And the people are ALL extremely friendly and supportive etc.

This is VR as good as it can get with TONS of fun and infinite things to do. Seriously it's mind-blowingly good.

name: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt
review:
Quite simply if you're an open world action RPG fan, this is the greatest game of all time. What CDPR managed to achieve in 2015 with their ambition being this high is nothing short of miraculous. All western open world RPG's will be compared to Witcher 3 for all time as the benchmark for storytelling, compelling side quests, player agency, non condescending scripts and themes, masculinity, grittiness, art design, music composition, and world building. 

The game is grim dark, it is shades of grey and forlorn despair for the most part just like our world. Very few choices you will make in this game are cut and dry, you will agonise over what decision to make even in side quests because they are so morally ambiguous. Every single decision you make in this game has repercussions and affects the world around you, someone you handed over to the guards you may find hanging from a tree a week later as you ride through the countryside, or being burned alive to jeering crowds (and this is only if by chance you happen upon the place where these consequences play out, you may never see them or know what outcome some decisions you made had, it is organic and beautiful this way), what seems like the altruistic decision at the time during a quest may lead to many innocents being slaughtered later. The player agency in this game cannot be understated, it is phenomenal and the game genuinely stirred up my human empathy and compassion, regret at times. Honestly, I don't know how CDPR made a game of this calibre and ten years later nothing has come even halfway near to what they achieved. 

It's 2025 and playing this in native 4K using the next gen graphics update settings I am constantly in absolute awe of this world, it is a monument of game art and a testament to a team of developers who clearly put their hearts and souls into this game. I am currently 113 hours in and by my estimates I have another 50 hours before I finish this play through and that doesn't include mopping up the last points of interest on the map. I know I will be returning to this game again, like I have now since I first played this MASTERPIECE (yes, this actually is a masterpiece, no exaggeration) in 2015. Playing through Witcher 2 and 3, and being part of Geralt's story is something I will carry with me the rest of my days, I feel like I know the characters and countries in this world.

name: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt
review:
After 9 hours i still do not know how any of the main game mechanics work. I think you need to have played games like this, or previous versions of this game. There are just way too many things that are assumed to be understood.

I have not reached a point in this game where i feel i know what i am doing, or what i am supposed to do. Most of it has been playing along with the "script", going to markers and accidentally stumbling on side quests.

I have not made any weapons up to this point, because i do not know how to find the ingredients needed, or how to get the coins needed. I do not know what weapons to make if i could, or how i can see if they were worth it if i could make any. I ended up just doing quests, hoping to get coins to craft something.

The combat system is like flipping a coin. Attack sometimes works, sometimes doesn't. Jumping out of the way sometimes works, sometimes doesn't.

I don't know if, when or how i should be using which sign. The q button does not work consistently for me, so even though the game says i can use signs in combat, i cannot. I am probably missing something here, but i can't tell.

I found out i can have bombs because a quest told me i needed some kind of bomb. I have no idea how to get bombs, or if they are better than melee weapons. If i had a bomb, i would probably not be able to find it in the menu, or be able to figure out how to equip it or use it.

I am currently in a quest with the basic weapons, where i am instantly killed by a wraith. It could be i need some protection against his one shot kill, but i do not know what that would be. I also don't know how to get out of the location where this wraith is.

Googling questions and watching other people play the game in order to make me be able to play the game is too much hassle, and not enjoyable at all.

I assume this game is great if you are familiar with the mechanics.

name: The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt
review:
The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt is an outstanding open-world role-playing game developed by CD Projekt Red. From the very first moments, the game captivates with its rich storytelling, immersive world, and deep character development.

You play as Geralt of Rivia, a monster hunter searching for his adopted daughter while navigating a war-torn world full of political intrigue, moral dilemmas, and dangerous beasts. The narrative is mature, branching, and full of emotional depth. Every choice you make has consequences, making each playthrough feel unique.

The graphics are breathtaking — from dense forests and bustling cities to stormy seas and eerie ruins. The soundtrack complements the world beautifully, and the voice acting, especially Geralt’s, adds life and authenticity to the characters.

Combat is fluid and strategic, blending swordplay, magic (signs), alchemy, and monster hunting tactics. The game also includes an expansive crafting and upgrade system, as well as the addictive card game Gwent.

With its massive world, gripping storyline, and attention to detail, The Witcher 3 sets a high standard for RPGs. It’s a must-play for any fan of fantasy or immersive storytelling.

Rating: 10/10

An extraordinary experience elevated by the loveliest fantasy universe I've had the honor of discovering.

The Witcher 3 is an abundant source of amazement with its gorgeous explorable worlds as well as its long list of intricate characters ; some loved, some begging for a silver sword through the thorax. 
Break free from the expected political neutrality as you delve into the labyrinth of dilemmas left & right. (I swear that pun wasn't intended.) 
Your sword won't be the only thing getting wet, as all the sorceresses in your viscinity will. Geralt has a knack for such things. Mixing monster hunting with pleasure never actually hurt anyone, right? So does having sex with at least 50% of the female roster.

Jest aside, I've never had more fun with an RPG ever before in my life. This is a masterpiece, and I doubt many will argue with that. The side quests either add additional layers to the characters' already complex personalities, or make you die of laughter. There are rare exceptions I can think of off the top of my head, but hey, no game's perfect ; however the positive overwhelmingly outweighs the negative.

This entry has gotten me into the franchise, as I'm playing the 2007 and 2011 entries. When you encounter a world as rich as this one is, you can't help but seek more in the source material : Sapkowski's The Last Wish, Time of Contempt and so on.

You will not regret this. This has been a crucial gaming experience that has affected me so positively that i'll forever smile at the mention of it.

Fall Guys delivers a refreshing take on the battle royale genre, trading realistic graphics and violence for chaotic, whimsical fun. Its colorful obstacle course design and quick match pacing make it easy to jump in and play, while still offering enough challenge to keep players engaged. The game's approachable mechanics and unpredictable outcomes contribute to its broad appeal, attracting players of all skill levels. It succeeds in creating a lighthearted, competitive experience that feels distinct in the crowded online multiplayer space.
Gameplay in Fall Guys is both accessible and addictive, relying on simple controls and chaotic physics to deliver laughter and frustration in equal measure. Each round introduces a new mini-game, ranging from races to team challenges, that test players' timing, coordination, and sometimes sheer luck. The randomness of physics-based movement and the unpredictability of other players contribute to a sense of constant surprise and excitement. Frequent content updates and rotating game modes help maintain the game’s replayability.
Visually, Fall Guys is bursting with charm. The jellybean-like characters and candy-coloured environments create a joyful aesthetic that perfectly matches the game’s light tone. Its use of soft textures, vibrant palettes, and playful animations ensures that even defeat feels less punishing and more amusing. The overall visual design enhances the experience by immersing players in a cartoonish world that never takes itself too seriously.
Overall, "Fall Guys" stands out as a unique and enjoyable party game experience that thrives on chaos and charm. Its lack of a story is more than made up for by entertaining gameplay and strong visual design. The combination of simplicity and unpredictability ensures that no two matches feel the same, and the game remains engaging across multiple sessions. It’s a polished, feel-good title that continues to delight with its upbeat energy and constant variety.

So long, Gearbox. You won't be missed.

name: Euro Truck Simulator 2
review:
Extremely chill and satisfying truck driving simulator. 

You go about the whole of Europe driving from point A to point B, yet the the game's all about the journey, not the destination. Simplicity is its biggest strength, and while I would never ever get behind a truck wheel in real life, here it seems pretty awesome to do so.

Some light RPG elements are in to keep you hooked, lots of customization and progression-based unlocks to be seen, plus there's a whole new world that's about to open to you as soon as you realize the game supports modifications. WELL DONE! And if the workshop doesn't sate your appetite, there are dedicated websites to all kinds of crazy mods out there.

I remember when this game came out in 2012, it was not that much better than ETS 1, was just OK. But the devs clearly kept on updating it all the way  to 2025, and now it looks just as good as it feels playing. Do make sure to get it on sale (not just the base game) as the DLCs can get pricey otherwise, even when bundled.

And one more thing, I leave you with a quote from the cult film Snatch:

Airport security guy: "Anything to declare?"
Dennis Farina as cousin Avi: "Yeah. Don't go to England."

review:
This game looks like it was made from the unity asset store, the animations look like an afterthought, the STUPID stamina system is so annoying. The level up system feels like it does jack and takes forever to level up, it gives runescape a run for it's money. I can not tell the difference between level 1 woodcutting and level 30 woodcutting. You can easily cheat on servers if you have use mods (happened to me.) The art-style is way too clashing, you got a oddly looking skeleton and a weird tree thingy that looks like they were taking *cough cough* straight out of the unity asset store. I am pretty sure I've seen Xbox 360 Indie games look and play better than this.
You have to grind so long to get basically anywhere, you want a pickaxe, go kill a boss. You want a better pickaxe? Go find a skeleton structure with those annoying minecraft skeletons just to find a cores for smelters... and several other skeletons. Then you into the deep forest to find "special" rocks to get copper (which weighs a lot). Then, you have to have to go find tin along the higher level shorelines is great (because it ways a lot). Then you gotta deal with the smelter part which you can only get (at that level) charcoal from burning food. After you get Bronze, you can sacrifice one to FINALLY make a cart... so you can quicken the process of getting more copper and tin.
The combat is so boring, they do a lot of damage, you do jack to some of the enemies, while other can literally one tap you *cough cough* shaman early game with that stupid poison that does a guaranteed 40-50 damage until you get middle game potions to stop it. If their is a horde, you get hit and you get stagger, guaranteed death. I also love the logic of parrying a projectile staggers the attacker... somehow. Attacking feels way too slow, Your swinging can take a full seconds which doesn't really help when they are attacking you a bit faster. If you don't get a stagger in them, you are basically hit. The AI pathfinding is so annoying, they either oddly run around you which just leaves with you chasing them while some go full on aggression leaving you no time for safe attacks.
Honestly Muck is more entertaining than this... and that's free. The building aspect is quite nice but the base decay is so annoying due to rain or water plus you get jack from cutting trees down. 
Also I had this annoying bug when trying to join servers where is just wouldn't let me, just said fail to connect. It just randomly let's me in servers sometimes.

TLDR: Looks cheap, annoying systems, long grinds, bad combat, and poor AI.

review:
Over 700 in-game days and 290 real hours... Why have I stopped at this particular moment? I've built quite a large base protected with balistas, I've grown (almost) all types of crops, I've tried out (almost) all the building materials, I've upgraded all types of weapons and armor for (almost) each age to its maximum, I've completed the Hildir's Request (collected all 9 chests of all 3 types), I've defeated the Queen in the Mistlands, I've built Drakkar, took all the necessary materials to build Shield generators and set sail to the Ashlands, I've encountered two Bonemaws that damaged the ship by half and five Voltures before even going ashore, I've finally approached the shore... right next to the Monument of Torment, and I've finally died from Charred Warriors' hits that surrounded me - they've destroyed my wooden portal and, most likely, Drakkar with the loot on it - my best armor and weapons remained in the tombstone in the hellscape. At this point I realized I've spent enough time on all this and it's high time to move on.

I played only few sandbox games, but from the ones I did play, Valheim is undoubtedly the best one. After this much of playing I can't say I have any complains regarding gameplay - I really liked all the aspects of it. It was a pleasure to explore new biomes with its own flora and fauna, dangeons, bosses, crafting options, to establish my own base and constantly upgrade it, to tame animals and prepare different types of food.

I'm looking forward to the Deep North update - the moment when the game probably leaves Early Access and it will contain everything the developers wanted for the full release. I don't rule out the chance that I'll return to the game, especially with the release of a new biome.

"Where the grass grows underfoot,
And the sky is blue overhead,
There will always be a hearth and a home"

review:
I absolutely love this game. It is simple yet does what it wants to, VERY well. After about 100 hours I can confidently say that this has been the best experience playing a survival game, out of all I've played. The gameplay is challenging, yet rewarding. I played through the entire ashlands biome and loved it all. 

The positive: My favorite part of the game is the atmosphere and score. The music is beautiful and fits every biome it is played in. The building takes some getting used to but once you figure it out, you can build extravagant and beautiful viking-inspired homes. The looting and dungeon crawling is nicely done. The passive skill system is a grind but you really do feel the difference in damage and speed when you put time into your character. The visuals are stunning and are really what hooked me on the game in the first place.

The needed improvements: I do wish there were more QoL settings to where you would not need mods to make the game less frustrating at times - I'm looking at you mistlands! The variety in the world is a bit disappointing and I would love to see more to do in each biome, perhaps some named mini bosses or better and more rewarding loot. I would really love to see an active skill tree that allows for more character variety to really hone the RPG aspect of the game. 

Overall, the game in its current state is very polished and with every update, the game improves upon itself. I would 10/10 recommend the game to any who are wishing to get lost in an atmospheric, punishing world!

I have never seen anything in all of my time playing games.
Despite limiting frames via V-sync or the Nvidia Control panel, switching the overall graphical settings to medium, trying DX or Vulkan and performing all other steps recommended online the game causes SEVERE GPU temperatures, despite it staying on 30-45% utilization.
Additionally, there's an incomprehensible load on the PC in the Main Menu, with temperatures easily exceeding 80C, on a well ventilated Desktop that does not break 75C playing Cyberpunk 2077 on mixed HIGH/ULTRA, another comparison I can give is that Star Citizen runs smoother with less generated heat.
CPU is also at 25-35% yet the game experiences severe stutters unable to hold a solid 60, made even more apparent with the new Overlay Performance Monitor. If it isn't apparent from the screenshots, while I enjoy the style of the graphics the end product does NOT warrant such extreme strain on the hardware.


Because of the online discourse on the topic of this game's performance and several cases of hardware malfunction following prolonged play and the inexplicable ratio of GPU load to GPU temperature I've personally observed - I consider this game to be dangerous piece of software that puts your hardware at risk long term. And no, my hardware is not the issue, nor is the hardware of other people who I've seen gaslit on every mention of the game's performance. There are plenty of people with better and/or worse hardware than mine on both Nvidia and AMD, this is not a hardware issue, this is a Valheim issue.
My recommendation is that the game should either be taken down from the store or must come with a warning of potential severe hardware degradation and even failure following prolonged play - as the first thing one sees in the store page. 

I'm familiar with this game's content and it's one I believe to be up there in both quantity and quality, combat is fluid and responsive, however, the developers should focus on fixing performance in general and making sure that it's even across the board and doesn't vary as much as it does when changing biomes / encountering specific enemies. 

I really wanted to give it a fair go and go though the content myself and not as a viewer, however, I will not risk my hardware because the Developers have prioritized putting more content and reaching 1.0 faster, potentially raising the price because it's now "complete".

TL:DR - Great game kneecapped by shocking lack of optimization after several years in development.

review:
The game demands a high level of cognitive engagement and strategic thinking from the player. Success relies on your ability to analyze subtle environmental clues, interpret audio and visual evidence, and synthesize that data to correctly identify the type of ghost you're dealing with. It's not just about observation—it's about deductive reasoning, pattern recognition, and making informed decisions under pressure. Additionally, the game tests your survival instincts in real-time; as the haunting intensifies, maintaining composure while navigating increasingly dangerous situations becomes critical. The blend of logical puzzle-solving with adrenaline-pumping horror creates an incredibly immersive and mentally stimulating experience.

This game is truly a masterpiece with lots of potential. The mechanics are easy to learn, but might be hard to master. Just take your time... It offers different difficulty levels, and you can even customize the experience with your own settings to make it even more of a nightmare.

It's highly recommended to play with friends, as many people do not want to play with newbies, so prepare yourself to get kicked from the lobby. 

Don't forget to support your local game developer companies! Thank you, Kinetic Games.

name: Paladins
review:
Ah Paladins - you truly were something special. So why did I hate playing you half the time?

These things are complicated... I'll say this - there's never been a multiplayer game I've played where there was so much toxicity. Why should this be the case? 

- Frustration with bad matchmaking - people get sick of most matches being a "stomp" one way or the other
- No incentive to continue fighting a losing match - some people just stay in spawn and wait to re-queue for the next as soon as they get a whiff of a loss (leading them to hate even more on those struggling on and prolonging the torture)
- Balance issues? If you die to X or Y "imba" attack/character enough times it feels bad - balancing could have been better, but asymmetrical games will always have this issue to one extent or another.
- Free game = free account = people not worried about being banned for toxicity? (were such bans even ever a thing??)
- No option to mute people by default - you have to do it manually at the start of every match (and then you'll still see hate in the post-match lobby - maybe even directed at you causing serious ego bruising)
- Small teams meant 1 bad player on your team could likely make you lose (so people hated that) (maybe games should've been 10v10?)
- The game's card system while being one of its best features also encouraged experimentation - meaning sometimes players were trying out something new and not performing well
- Matchmaking was account-based rather than character based - so you could be amazing at one or two or even 10 characters, but if trying a new character which plays radically differently, you'll still be matched against the same calibre of players (games could be decided by whether people were playing familiar characters or trying new ones)

In short, people hated playing when they were losing, because you'd get wrecked - close matches (where the real fun was) were rare. And in a game where you lose 50% of the time, that means someone's raging 50% of the time. Rage reminds you that you're wasting your life playing video games with kids or immature adults. This ruins the escapism and reminds you that YOU are an immature adult and should be doing something better with your time - like exercising or investing in Nvidea.

review: This was a fun game even before Overwatch's... decline, but now that the once-vaunted king of hero shooters has irrevocably proven itself to be one of the most legendarily mishandled projects in the medium, it seems it's time for Paladins to really shine. I will say that while it's fine and dandy that the majority of these little loot box items can be directly bought, I feel as though the actual prices are a bit high for what you're getting. name: NARAKA: BLADEPOINT
review:
As someone who’s tried almost every battle royale under the sun, I can honestly say Naraka: Bladepoint stands out – and not just because of its flashy visuals or fast combat. It’s one of those rare games where, even after getting stomped a few times, you want to queue back in, get better, and land those satisfying kills.

- Graphics & Art Style
Right off the bat, Naraka hits you with style. The game has this beautiful mix of ancient Eastern aesthetics with a bit of high-fantasy flair. Environments are varied – from cherry blossom forests to misty temples – and they actually feel alive.
What I like most is the character design. Every hero looks unique, their animations are smooth, and special abilities have a nice visual pop without being overdone. Also: runs super smooth, even on mid-tier PCs.

- Gameplay & Combat
Combat is the selling point. If you’re into melee-focused games, this is a playground.
Movement feels buttery smooth, with grappling hooks, parkour, wall-running, and verticality baked into every map.
The combat system is timing-based, almost like a fighting game – think rock-paper-scissors, but with blades, combos, and counters. Every kill feels earned. Button mashers don’t get far. Ranged weapons are there too (bows, muskets, cannons), but melee is the star of the show. There’s a learning curve, no doubt. But once you land your first perfect counter or chain kill, you're hooked.

- Heroes & Abilities
Each hero brings something different – some are tanks, others are stealthy assassins, and some support your squad.
Abilities aren’t overpowered like in some hero-based games; they enhance your playstyle without replacing mechanical skill.

- Modes & Match Variety
Standard solo, duo, trio BR modes Ranked for competitive grind Limited-time events, custom lobbies, and a PvE mode for chill sessions. Also includes a cool tutorial and training mode for mastering combos or weapons

- Sound & Music
Audio is top-notch. Weapon swings are crisp, footsteps matter (especially in sweaty 1v1s), and the soundtrack has a cinematic, East-Asian vibe that fits the theme perfectly. Some character voice lines can be a bit cheesy, but it’s part of the charm.

- Customization & Progression
Skins, weapons, armor – a lot of cosmetic depth, and it doesn't feel too pay-to-win.
The monetization is there, but not aggressive. Most stuff can be earned by just playing. And they drop new skins and heroes often enough to keep it fresh.

- What I Don’t Love (But Can Live With)
New players might feel overwhelmed at first Matchmaking can be rough at certain MMRs
Some balance issues pop up now and then after patches
But to be fair, the devs are active, drop regular updates, and listen to community feedback more than most.

- Final Verdict
Naraka: Bladepoint isn’t just a gimmick BR – it’s a legitimately fun, stylish, and skill-based brawler that rewards good timing, smart movement, and tactical decisions. If you’ve ever wished Apex or Fortnite had swords, this is your game.

Score: 8.5 / 10
Great game with a steep skill ceiling, killer visuals, and actual staying power.

name: NARAKA: BLADEPOINT
review:
I've been playing this game on & off for around 4 years (this will be the 4th, as I was D1)
A lot of time was spent in the beta servers or PS.

This game came out at a terrible time, being the craze and hype of Apex, Val and resurgence of Fortnite.
It kept to it's community which MY GOODNESS is AMAZING. The devs are constantly taking criticism and talk with their community via various media platforms and it's shaped up to be a REALLY good BR. If not one of the best. 

Naraka sports an EXTREMELY HARD learning curve and it will take time to learn weapon combos, movement combos and character combos. That seems like a lot, because it is.. The characters you play work better with various weapons, till you play long enough to vet and interchange weapons with the characters without any issues. Combos in this game are key once you get into ranked, more so the higher side of ranked. That alone takes the cake for me, as I play fighting games a lot and find myself competing in tournaments as well. To tie into the community aspect, they have Dojos via their Discord, which are essentially people well versed in the game, who are open to coaching you on all aspects of Naraka, whether it be Characters, weapons or movement. (pretty Neat right!) 

Events are very frequent, normally having a handful each season, which snag you nice costumes for your weapons and characters, items to open lootboxes or help with your ranked/showdown experience. The only stinker is that they are all limited events and only some select things from those events stay in shops for you to buy said skins, so this game, like many others are BIG in Fomo. 

Along with the events, each season comes with a lootbox pool (or banner for my gacha players), which can snag you EVEN MORE outfits outside of what is offered in the Battle Passes. I often find myself lost in the amount of cool things each lootbox offers, but these can always be opened even beyond the date of the season pass, which I think is amazing, because if you miss out during the season, you aren't locked out from those items, though they are harder to get the specific boxes to unlock them.. so it's a trade off and one i'm not complaining over. 

The characters themselves are fresh and come with unique skill sets and full of personality. Another feature that Naraka has Introduced into the BR scene, is the ability to fully customize EACH and EVERY character to your liking, as if you were playing an MMO, which I've never seen done in a BR, to this scale and I absolutely find myself spending a good couple hours creating themed outfits for my mains.

I find it cool that a game like this exists as it's been something that I've wanted for a while, as the other BR games are cliche (fps wise). You have to truly learn the game and adapt to different situations. I'd highly recommend this game if you enjoy a challenge and even more so if you enjoy fighting games, or games with good movement. Though do be weary that your first couple of games will be bots and past that you'll get thrown in with high ranking players, as it's going to be casual play only. 

Naraka has a great solo "story mode" called Showdown, which I myself never tried till recently and want to slap myself for not doing so when it came out about a year or so ago. Also great practice for new players as it's PVE only. 

Other than that, some items are easy to come across, While others will take you a fair amount of time to acquire. You get a lot of nice goodies when starting out, but there are a decent (understatement) amount of purchasable skins, which unfortunately are pretty costly, but do go on discount rotation quite frequently. 

TLDR- Give it a shot if you enjoy fighting games, character customizing and BRs, but expect to put time into it to learn through it's steep curve.

While it features satisfying physics-based gameplay and the signature Gravity Gun mechanics, the overall reception is mixed compared to other shooters. name: Half-Life
review:
I realise this is heresy (and makes me look like a hipster), but I don't care. This legend was just not fun for me, and not in a "it aged poorly" kind of way. The game's aged great, I just don't like it. Here's the details, with comparisons to games of the era:

- "Jumpscare enemies": Along the golden path are enemies that you don't have any way of knowing are there 75% of the time. It starts with headcrabs and escalates from there. Kills the pacing of the game. Some games from then have them, some don't. At least Unreal would warn you about jumpscare Skaarj with that laugh.
- Speaking of escalating, if you don't know where every weapon is, enemies get very spongy by endgame, and you have little health and less ammo. Unreal, Deus Ex, and GoldenEye keep your kit relevant the whole game, even if you don't use it all.
- There's not a single thing for this one, but the level Blast Pit and the Surface Tension Ordinance depot both really got under my skin. Partly lack of information, partly stacked failstates (like Headcrabs right next to laser mines that blow up the level).
- Turret bunkers: the military gets sandbag bunkers with manned turrets that I couldn't figure out how to destroy, only take out the gunner... except in order to do that, you have to grenade into the bunker or get close and almost die. At least other games would let you blow up the guns.
- Mandatory damage: imo, terrible design to require damage on the golden path. I was fed up when on Surface Tension you have to slide down a pipe... that triggers fall damage when you hit the flange, almost 25  pts worth. Can't recall a single instance in Unreal or GoldenEye where it was required to take damage to progress.
- Movement, platforming and ladders: So, back in the day there was no great solution for ladders. The movement in this game, though, makes the other two miserable. Freeman must have wheels on his HEV, because that's exactly how slippery movement felt. If I strafed while moving it was just like skating. Which makes platforming extra miserable, and sends you flying off ladders. My first damage of the game was literally the first ladder, I went flying off and took fall damage. In literally every other game I've played from that era, you just stopped when you let go of W, you didn't slide three extra feet. If you think I'm exaggerating, find a staircase and just tap D, you slide right down to the bottom. This also compounds onto combat problems because it makes dodging less responsive.

One final note: I know what games were like in 1998 because I was there. I know exactly how games have changed since then, and I'd still rather play Unreal or GoldenEye over HL1. I'm hoping HL2 will be better.

name: Half-Life
review:
Half-Life, released by Valve in 1998, stands as a groundbreaking milestone in the history of first-person shooters and narrative-driven gaming. Combining innovative gameplay mechanics, immersive storytelling, and atmospheric design, Half-Life redefined what a shooter could be and set new standards for the genre. The game casts players as Gordon Freeman, a theoretical physicist caught in the middle of a catastrophic experiment gone wrong at the Black Mesa Research Facility. What follows is a tense and thrilling journey filled with alien invasions, government cover-ups, and desperate survival against both extraterrestrial creatures and hostile military forces. Unlike many shooters of its era, Half-Life integrates its narrative seamlessly into gameplay, eschewing traditional cutscenes for in-engine scripted sequences that keep players fully immersed in the unfolding story.

The level design in Half-Life is meticulously crafted to foster exploration, puzzle-solving, and strategic combat, creating a fluid and engaging experience that feels both cinematic and interactive. The game’s AI was revolutionary at the time, with enemies that use tactics such as flanking and seeking cover, heightening the intensity of encounters. Weapons feel distinct and impactful, from the iconic crowbar to experimental energy guns, encouraging players to adapt their approach to different combat scenarios. The pacing strikes a fine balance between moments of frenetic action, suspenseful tension, and quieter exploration, maintaining player engagement throughout the game’s progression.

What truly distinguishes Half-Life is its storytelling approach, which embeds the narrative directly into the environment and player experience. The game world is rich with detail—from scientists and security personnel reacting believably to the crisis, to scattered notes and visual cues that deepen the lore. This storytelling method allows players to piece together the bigger picture at their own pace, fostering a sense of discovery and immersion rarely seen before. The atmospheric sound design, haunting music, and visual effects further enhance the mood, making Black Mesa feel like a living, breathing facility under siege.

Half-Life’s impact extends beyond its gameplay and story; it revolutionized game development by inspiring countless developers and spawning a passionate modding community, eventually leading to the creation of titles like Counter-Strike and Portal. Its influence is still felt today in the design philosophies of modern shooters and narrative-driven games. While some aspects, such as graphics and controls, may feel dated by contemporary standards, the core gameplay and storytelling remain timeless.

In summary, Half-Life is not just a first-person shooter but a transformative experience that elevated the medium to new heights. Its innovative design, immersive narrative, and intelligent AI set a benchmark that shaped the future of gaming. For players seeking a challenging, atmospheric, and deeply engaging adventure, Half-Life offers an unforgettable journey into a sci-fi world where survival depends on wit, skill, and courage. It remains a must-play classic and a shining example of how games can tell compelling stories while delivering thrilling action.

Rating: 9/10

First off, the game looks amazing. The monsters are huge, detailed, and just straight-up badass. The environments feel alive, and every hunt is an adventure. But what really caught me is how smooth the combat feels, especially once you get into a rhythm with your weapon of choice. It’s got depth, but it doesn’t feel overwhelming.
Now, I know a lot of people used to avoid this game because of the grind. And yeah, it was a bit much at launch. But honestly? That’s really changed. You can progress a lot easier now without spending hours upon hours farming the same monster. It’s way more friendly to new and casual players.
I was so into it that I grabbed the Iceborne DLC too—and I’m glad I did. Not only does it add a ton of new content, but it also introduces the Clutch Claw (a grapple mechanic), which adds a cool layer to combat. It lets you combo into monsters better and just feels super satisfying to use.

If you’re picking this up now, the bundle is such a good deal. You can get the base game plus the DLC for like ₹999, which is a steal for the amount of content you're getting. Honestly, the game is easily a 9.5/10 for me.
Whether you’re a long-time fan or someone curious to jump in, Monster Hunter: World is totally worth your time now. Just be ready to fall in love with hunting giant monsters.

[h1]Monster Hunter: World + Iceborne – 100% Completion Review[/h1]
[i]All achievements earned, every monster hunted and captured, all weapon trees completed, every event quest cleared, all layered armor unlocked[/i]

[b]Monster Hunter: World is the series’ breakthrough moment — an uncompromising ecosystem built for mastery, not accessibility.[/b]
Completing everything is not just a test of patience. It is a test of understanding, adaptation, and raw skill.

Each monster is a biome in motion, with distinct behaviors, tells, and attack patterns. Weapons are entire playstyles. A longsword plays nothing like a hammer. A bow is a different game entirely. The loop is simple: hunt, carve, forge. But beneath that is a web of mechanics that rewards commitment.

[b]Iceborne is a full sequel in all but name.[/b]
It raises the ceiling on difficulty and introduces the clutch claw, a high-risk, high-reward mechanic that reshapes combat flow. Master Rank monsters hit harder, behave differently, and force you to rethink everything you learned in the base game.

[b]The postgame is absurdly deep.[/b]
Guiding Lands, event quests, investigations, and decorations add hundreds of hours of grind with just enough variance to keep it interesting. Earning every achievement means confronting tempered variants, arch-tempered beasts, and layered armor grinds that demand total mechanical fluency.

The game respects your time only if you respect the systems. Everything has weight. Every potion matters.

name: Heroes & Generals
review:
I'm afraid I cannot recommend this game. I tried, I played it for a while and I might continue to play it (in a more limited way), but honestly I think I'm done.

There are a few technical problems with the game:
Performance of the game varies highly between updates. I got anything from sustained 60 fps (with vsync on) at high quality setting to 20-25 on the lowest quality.
Weird lag issues. Game freezes momentarily on certain occasions, sometimes at crucial events, eg. just before being killed. This is not related to CPU or memory nor GFX card. I doubt it's network related. If it is, it's server side.

The game also feels a bit unbalanced. If enemy has air superiority, you're doomed. As ground unit there's not a lot you can do. This brings me to the next frustrating fact: you have several characters each has several weapons. You cannot swap [strike]characters or[/strike] weapons during a match. You have to leave the match, leave the squad and then you can swap weapons.

[i]EDIT: apparently you can swap characters if you have more than one of the same class. Thanks to RooZ for bringing this up. I haven't tested it, though. Swapping for a different class is possible if the squad has proper slots[/i]

There's a lot of griding as many have said. Personally I don't mind griding per se. What  I do mind is having to play for extended amount of time at a severe disadvantage. So either you pay money to upgrade fast or you are basically working for Reto as unpaid cannon fodder for their paying customers. In some games if you're good you may get a fighting chance. But not here. As infantry - yes. As tank crewman, not really. You will be put against superior tanks that you cannot harm with your puny cannon. And when you die you'll have to wait before spawning again and then walk or drive for a while to get to the action. There's a lot of waiting and walking in this game. I guess that makes it a more realistic military simulation. ;)

The grind is the price of a free game you say. Fair enough. However this game also suffers from the same problems as any other FPS, free or not. The lack of teamplay. When I first started playing H&G I saw how team actions (capturing) actually gives you significantly more score points compared to just killing an enemy. I said "wonderful, they found a way to make people actually do objectives". Sadly I was mistaken. Points schmoints. There are still very few people who will actively engage in coordinated cooperative gameplay. You'll get a circle of campers just outside capture zone. People will use resources without considering they're limited and waste them. Tank drivers will not rotate tanks so that support gunners may engage targets. Vehicles with MGs are never parked with their guns facing enemy positions. A fair amount will not follow common sense regarding objective selection and some will even roam aimlessly around the map.

I'd gladly pay money for a game with a nice teamplay-oriented community but this one isn't it.

So, should you play this free game? After all I said I might continue. If you do, stick to infantry, most vestatile, easiest to survive. Get a car or a motorbike to get from spawn area to the action. If you go for any other class, expect a lot more grinding and consider that your leveling strategy and point investment may be subverted by game designers at any point.
