review:
I would find it very hard to give this game a positive review, unless of course you like being endlessly spawn camped, playing on wildly mismatched teams, and having the game devs constantly "tweaking" the game to make it more (not really) "playable".

Let me first bring up the un even team issue. For some unknown to me reason , most of the new players of this game start playing on the American faction. In my experience in the game ( over 1k hours atm) this seems to be a constant. So if you want to join and you are new try the Soviet side. I cant for personall reasons play or reccommend the Nazi faction. When you play this seems to be one of the largest problems, if you have experience most of your team won't. The game match system to keep the teams even fairly balanced in staged matches seems hopelessly broken with teams loaded with players with large in game experience vs. teams with very little. This is to be somewhat expected in the war mode of play but not in staged.

  If you like to play as a tanker you can, not really sure how you start this now, I've had a tanker character from beta when you just switched (it does cost in game credits) from an infantry to a tanker and start working your way up. Being a tanker can be fun at times but the inconsistency makes it tough. Then of course there are the AT clowns. We regulars have alot of names for them, rambos, commandoes, you get the idea. If you are in a tank especially a heavy, you are pretty much hosed. The lowest AT guy (anti tank) can carry mines or stickies, the mines they run up to you from behind place the mine on you and then shoot it, boom your dead. This wouldn't matter too much except that you have to pay for your tank spawns. Now as a high level tanker you can afford this, but as a low level tanker you lose credits, and it can be very expensive. The heavy tanks are especially susceptable to these attacks as they do not move faster than any infantry can move at a walk.

Lets move on to the spawn camping: It does exist in almost every mulitplayer online game but i've never played a game where it is as widespread as this game. Every so often the devs change a few things on the maps to make it more difficult but when you cant leave the spawn in a tank, truck or jeep its a serious problem.  

Then I will bring up the devs:  For some reason when the game was in beta we had some pretty good maps with varied terrain and options for a lot of play styles. Yes these maps had some problems but instead of addressing the problems they made entirely new maps! WITH THE SAME PROBLEMS! Now i dont want to bash the guy who made them, they are pretty big and complex with quite a bit of detail but the management team that pushed this, needs to have their collective heads examined.  When you have thousands of players giving feedback about issues there has to be some really common threads, address them. Now for some other reason there are no published stats about the weapons you are using in game. For example how much damage does rifle x do with mod a c and e, or how much actual armor will this tank shell penetrate. Tank shells bounce off targets with alarming frequency, depending on who you are fighting. I would not have issue with this but they seem to not have considered that each shell might hit the tank or may have been aimed so as to hit the armor at 90 degrees for penetration.  For example a german tiger 2 is nearly impentrable from the front or sides even if you hit the sloping armor not at an angle but at 90 degrees. I've hit them myself many times when the first shot will penetrate and every subsequent shot will bounce off the exact same spot. One or two time I could understand but five while that tank is stationary? The devs also constantly tweak your equipment so as soon as you get used to it they nerf it and well its useless.  They seem to do this with most every piece of equipment in the game, tank armor, speed, shell penetration, manueverablity, same with rifles. Don't get used to what you have, next week it will be crap.

The devs have also got some really weird stuff going on with the strategy side of the game that greatly affects gameplay on the first person shooter side. If a general has an Assault Team with low stats (like vision) you cant see the enemy very well while you play, yeah I did say that you might be fighting guys that are very hard to see, likewise if you have a good AT stats your team can destroy the enemy like nothing. It makes for bizzare gameplay.  I do not know if that is what causes so many people who play this to call hacks. Which is also as near as I can tell is also an issue. The devs say that they do anti hacking "sweeps" , sadly they do not do enough. I personally have watched playes on other teams use aimbots to shoot with perfect accuracy planes down with tanks from accross the map when the planes spawned. Wait let me rephrase that, THEY SHOT BEFORE THE PLANES SPAWN, and hit them 95% of the time as they became visible. I'm pretty sure i reported those 2 guys, saw them months later not banned, and was told by another player that "that guy is really good! Hes got a utube channel" to which I replied that he was cheating that I saw it on my own screen that there is no way to shoot that accurately with a tank from that distance.

Soo after that long, rambling review, for the reasons I stated and others I didn't, I can't reccommend investing your time into this game. Its sad that I say this because I am one of many who paid them actual money.

review: This game will break you before it rewards you. My first dozen characters died pathetically—starving because I couldn't find a can opener, bleeding out from a scratch I ignored, or getting swarmed after foolishly breaking a window. But that's when it clicked: Zomboid isn't about surviving the apocalypse, it's about learning how to stop being terrible at it. The sheer satisfaction of finally securing a safehouse, wiring it with generator power, and watching the hordes shamper past your carefully built defenses is unmatched. Yes, the graphics look like they're from 2012 and the UI fights you constantly, but no other game makes finding a damn cooking pot feel like striking gold. Just don't expect mercy—this is a brutal teacher that rewards patience and punishes every mistake with an embarrassing death screen.

Don't be fooled by the "bad" graphics, this game is FUN.

name: Project Zomboid
review:
I think this will be the first Steam review I have ever made. 

First off, I'd like to say that PZ has been close to my heart for many years. It's brought such lovely experiences, especially when playing with friends. Taking that into account, I have to give a thumbs down here. 

I started playing this game when I was first year in university. I'm now almost 30, and this game has evolved in many ways (I will not discount it for that), but not in a direction that makes much sense... All the core elements that make a fun zombie apocalypse game (bashing zombie heads, playing with friends, finding cool weapons and bases, etc...) have been pushed to the side for so long in favour of incredibly unnecessary add-ons that I don't see much use in (like pottery... why? In a zombie survival game? Instead of NPCs? Weird). 

Additionally, the community has become increasingly brainwashed to the point where they are spurring the devs to keep up their sub-par ways instead of promoting a want for a complete product (which is so way overdue). Guys, can we please be real? It's been over 12 years. That's... absolutely insane for ANY kind of game. The worst part? There still so much to be done! When will that actualize? 2055? When I'm 60? Come on...

It's with great sadness that I give a negative review, but I fear I'm at my wits end and have no alternative to influence a speed up in development time. 

To the 'white knights' that defend this game like it's their magnum opus, please understand. Some of us no longer have the chance to play this game with our friends like we used to (despite desperately wishing we could). It's now a dream that will never come true, and that hurts deeply. If you want to say, "just load b41 and play that again", then my response would be that "I shouldn't have to". We promised that we'd wait for b42 stable multiplayer before we conjoined again. I want to say 'we' are still waiting, but that 'we' became 'I', and now, alas, nobody. 

To the devs... For the love of everyone that treasures your beautiful game, please stop doing the unnecessary, and lock down on what you already have. It's more than enough. 

I don't aim to insult, ridicule, finger-point, or shame. I'm just a frustrated dude who really wanted to see this game reach its true state before having kids (not that I have them yet XD but I'm sure I will by the time this shiz stabilizes).

If you're still on the fence, you really shouldn't be. The game is just so genuinely well made and unique. review:
Storymode is perfect and there's nothing I would ask that needs to be changed. Graphics are beautiful, there are tons of detail in everything including the NPC interactions, even footprints and tracks you or your horse leave behind in the different elements. The story is unlike any I've ever come across and I love it so much. The only issue I have is with Red Dead Online mode.

The graphics are the same as storymode but it's the currency and leveling system which ruin it for me. It takes hours just to get 100 bucks and that's only if your wandering around looking for missions or hunting and selling all of the time. All of the things you'd want to buy; clothes, outfits, accessories & weapons are at INSANE prices and some you can't even buy without having GOLD which by the way is given out to you in decimals. If that isn't bad enough you can only unlock some clothes when you're at a certain level, some are easily lvl 40-60. That's with everything including the weapons and horses as well. Don't even get me started with the horses and weapons. You get stuck with a horrible horse when you first log in which while you can say that's fair, like I said with the money being so hard to get, some horses are easily 1000 dollars and some of them aren't even that good for a price like that. You would have to be spending many in real life days on the game just to buy a horse. You can try find some wild horses but they are just as bad as the one you log in with. If you want to do bounty's get money quick you'd need to pay 15-20 gold just to get a license to do it. WHAT? Arthur Morgan could do bounty's in storymode yet he didn't need a license. I get if its to make it so you have to work a bit harder online but hell.

The players are also an issue. Most of the players you find on there either try to kill you or your horse and your lucky they ignore you. You could just shoot back at them if it weren't for the fact the guns just don't work the same as they do in storymode. You have to shoot players twice as much and animals are worse, especially if your new to online and have the default guns that they give you. There are also so many mod menu users it's mad. Almost every session there's at least one that messes with me or my horse. I've had moments where I was walking my horse and randomly blew up. Not to mention my horse can get de-spawned randomly and at times I would get teleported off the saddle. I don't know if that last one was a modder doing that to me or if it was just a glitch but it was still very annoying nonetheless.

Anyways, those are my thoughts and opinions on RDR2. Hope you all the best.

The customization system is a huge step back from Reach. Remember how you could actually build your Spartan’s look without turning them into a walking neon billboard? Yeah, none of that here. Instead, you get these ugly, over-the-top cosmetics shoved down your throat — many locked behind grindy battle passes or insanely expensive bundles.

Speaking of the battle pass, it’s painfully slow and feels designed to squeeze you dry. The monetization is aggressive and clunky, making it clear that this isn’t about fun anymore — it’s about cash.

And the campaign? Honestly, it’s pretty forgettable. It lacks the punch and story depth of previous Halo games. Nothing really sticks with you once it’s done, which is a shame because that’s usually the series’ strong point.

Recently, the dev team has been super consistent with their content drops, and I hope they keep up the pace. The game is solid, but I can think of other games that have elements of Halo Infinite does, and executes better. And yet, I find myself coming back. Halo Infinite is the sum of it's parts. I recommend this game to anyone that grew up playing classic Halo, or is curious to see what the old-heads are so crazy about. 

Me personally, Halo Infinite has a firm place in my game rotation.

This is going to be a biased review as i'll admit i couldn't care less about the multiplayer/pvp gamemode and i've never actually cared to try it, but here goes.

Characters are great, there are some genuinely great interactions and little story moments that still stick with me, and the villains manage to completely avoid being pastiches of past halo villains and really feel like a genuine, new threat with complex motivations.

name: Halo Infinite
review:
Halo Infinite marks a stellar comeback for the iconic franchise, blending the classic Halo formula with modern gameplay innovations to deliver a thrilling, expansive shooter experience. From the moment you step into Master Chief’s boots, the game recaptures the magic that made the series a household name while pushing the saga forward in exciting ways.

The campaign is a standout, weaving a compelling story of mystery, loyalty, and survival against the backdrop of the fractured Halo ring, Zeta Halo. The narrative balances grand sci-fi spectacle with intimate moments, deepening the bond between Master Chief and the AI companion, “The Weapon.” The open-ended level design encourages exploration and tactical freedom, making each encounter feel fresh and dynamic.

Gameplay feels smooth and responsive, retaining the satisfying gunplay Halo is known for while introducing new tools like the versatile Grappleshot, which adds verticality and creativity to combat and traversal. Enemy AI is smart and challenging, keeping battles intense without feeling overwhelming.

Multiplayer returns to form with a robust suite of modes, classic maps, and a progression system that rewards skill and persistence. The free-to-play model makes it accessible, and constant updates ensure a lively, evolving community.

Visually, Halo Infinite strikes a balance between nostalgia and modernity, with beautiful, sprawling environments and detailed character models that run smoothly even on mid-range hardware.

If there’s a minor criticism, it’s that some side missions in the campaign can feel a bit repetitive, but overall, the pace and variety keep things engaging.

In summary: Halo Infinite is a brilliant blend of nostalgia and innovation, offering an unforgettable sci-fi shooter experience that honors the legacy of the franchise while boldly looking to the future. Whether you’re a veteran Spartan or a newcomer, this game delivers epic moments at every turn.

Rating: 7/10

I don't regret playing Raft or the money payed for it. But I am sadden that what should have been an excellent game, somehow fell this short. For me who loves this type of game, a "meh experience" is unexceptionable. So I can't recommend.

Ways to get soft-locked
1. Dieing without stored backup tools. Because you will loss them.
2. No, you can't start a new raft or build on land. No in-game reason is given.
3. Being unable to build a paddle, to push off that island you crashed into.

If you want a way to revive yourself without losing most of you stuff use "www.saveeditonline.com"
Your save file is at C:\Users\{Username}\AppData\LocalLow\Redbeet Interactive\Raft\User\User_{SteamUserID}\Player
Work out what "user" (I was 2) and change the values.
Users > 0 > Player > Health to value 1
Users > 0 > Player > Dead to value 0
After click on download at the bottom and replace the original file with the downloaded one. Restart game.

Also "https://www.raftmodding.com/" has a lot of good mods

For real though, Smite is a fun free2play Moba with really f***ing awesome abilites that will leave you in awe when you first see them. Oneshotting people by calling the kraken from the depths with posidon or seeing the enemy gods as small as literal ants while you stomp with Cuthulus ult through their ranks just feels incredible. name: World of Tanks Blitz
review:
Pretty entertaining for casual players. Faster crew member training than WoT(with or without golds). Lower xp requirements for tank research in tech trees. Faster paces of in-game experience. I think that's what "Blitz" is all about. Since it's "derived" from mobile platform(you can still play with mobile players), graphics performance can't compete with WoT but it's acceptable and getting better with every update(placebo maybe?)

Yes you can say it's a pay to win game since I can earn much more credits by playing tanks that are purchased with golds. Credits earned from those tanks can drastically accelerate your progress in techtrees. But honestly speaking, WoT and War thunder belong to that category as well. Either you spend a lot of time grinding for some particular tanks at certain levels that you're fond of, or you purchase in-game currency and speed up the process. The golds are on discount from time to time. So I'm pretty satisfied with it. 

I do hope WG can provide an exclusive HD graphics pack for PC players. The cooling fans of my gaming laptop never speed up when playing WOTB(i7-9750h+RTX 2080 max q)There're so much headroom that WOTB can squeeze out of average gaming laptop specs.

Edit(4/29/2020): 
Developers have justed added Girls und Panzer tanks in ALL SERVERS. Yes, you can buy Pz IV Ausf H, Tiger I & Hetzer that're originated from GuP TV animation. I really appreciate this decision cuz these tanks have been exclusive in Asia server for more than 4 years due to copyright reasons. Now not only can you purchase the collection in EU server(Russian server as well I guess), but two more tanks(IS-2 and Firefly) from the anime have been added to WOTB. Thx WG for showing the players and fans that you still care a lot about this project that you're in collaboration with after all these years.

name: Counter-Strike
review:
It was 2003.
I was nine years old—too young to understand recoil patterns, too young to know what "peeker's advantage" meant—but just old enough to feel the rush of a last-second defuse.

My older brother sat me down in front of our family’s bulky desktop, its fan whirring like a tired soldier. The monitor hummed, the keyboard clacked, and suddenly, I was in a world where nothing else mattered.

He loaded cs_assault, and I didn’t know the rules.
I didn’t know the callouts.
I didn’t even know which gun was "good."
But I knew the feeling—the electric jolt of a headshot, the panic of hearing footsteps behind me, the sheer weight of a round slipping away.

This wasn’t just a game.
It was a warzone where every second counted.

And then came the obsession.
The late nights spent memorizing grenade throws.
The way my hands shook clutching a cheap mouse in 1v1 clutch situations.
The maps weren’t just levels—they were battlefields I dreamed about.
I learned by dying.
By walking into my own Molotovs.
By planting the bomb in the wrong spot and getting screamed at in broken Russian over voice chat.
But every failure made me hungry.

My mother would sometimes pause in the doorway,
watching me lean closer to the screen like it might save me.
She didn’t get why I cared about terrorists and counter-terrorists.
But she let me have it—this place where skill mattered more than luck,
where every loss was a lesson, not just an ending.

Now, twenty years later, I still boot it up.
The textures are jagged.
The movement feels stiff compared to what’s out there now.
The community is a graveyard of forgotten aliases.

But something in Counter-Strike still lives.
The echo of an AK-47 bursting through a hallway.
The way your crosshair shakes when you’re the last one alive.
The maps—oh god, the maps—still humming with the ghosts of a thousand firefights.

Counter-Strike isn’t just a game.
It’s a time capsule.
A relic from when shooters weren’t about skins or ranks—
just grit, instinct, and the beautiful, brutal simplicity of outplaying someone.

And as I buy my Kevlar one more time,
as I step onto de_dust2 like it’s 2005 all over again,
I’m still there.
Fingers on WASD...
And a feeling I can’t quite place—
whether it’s longing, or just the quiet joy of coming home.

review:
TLDR: 3.8/5

To start off, I've been playing this game on/off since before official launch, I was actually a "Founder" for purchasing the founder pack waaaay long ago. It's accurate to say my experiences with this game are mostly positive, and I feel it's my duty to explain some of the points other people have in their reviews more in depth.

Starting off:

Pros: 
-Free
-Graphically flexible(can run on a bad pc or a great pc)
-Solid weapons, mechanics, etc.
-Compared to most BR games, this game still feels unique compared to others I've played.\
-Well designed maps
-Good character design


Cons:
-Bots?(see more later)
-Sometimes glitchy(mostly when jumping off high areas and trying to use the grappling hook. if the game stutters when doing this, you will die.
-Repetitive?(Usually the game is more or less locked to one map for a majority of the time, but it does change. also there are limited time game modes that appear, usually with a different map than the set map. Otherwise don't expect the set map to change more than once every season.

Now to get into some of the points up above. I'll start by saying that in addition to playing this game over a few years, currently (season 12) I've really enjoyed getting back into it and I am currently #22 in solo's in the game, so I would say its safe to say I more or less know what I'm talking about.

-Bots: I'm not too sure if they exist in the game, but I think it'd be safe to say that they do exist, and they do make the game a bit easy. I've never seen any official posts or patch notes regarding bots but I also never really kept up much with the game news since I play on/off a lot. Bots really just make the game lose appeal after a while, and as far as I can tell, it doesn't matter how good or bad you are, you might just get a game full of them, or with almost none. I'm ranked very high and I run into what I feel are bots very often. (more so in squads than in solo's) either that or the player base skill has really gone downhill.

-Desert Map/the season 10/11 catastrophe: This seems to be(from reviews/things I've heard from friends) to be pretty much the most hated map in ROE existence, but I would like to preface this saying that I've personally never played it, since I believe it was introduced in season 10 or 11, which I did not play during. Currently, in season 12, this map is not in rotation, so I have no gripes with it considering I pretty much love both the other maps. The game currently is not portrayed very well by the screenshots on steam, as almost all of them are season 11/10 which are basically widely hated(from my perspective) so I believe it is unfair to judge the game based on those few seasons/one map.

-Thoughts on current season compared to how I felt about previous seasons:
Honestly I've had a ton of fun playing this game this season, mainly because I can actually get into lobbies fairly quickly, very consistently. The main reason I played on/off was that usually the wait times for lobbies used to be extremely high(like 15 minutes to get into a game) The current season has no issues with this but I would probably attribute this due to the fact bots seem to be in the game now.
Season 1 was incredible for its time, offered a fresh new take on the BR genre and did it well. Season two introduced a new map: Europa Island, and a variety of new weapons, traversal options, customization items, etc. Season two was probably my all time favorite. Since then, I haven't noticed a whole ton of innovation to the game, as major changes only happen at the beginning of each season. The game seems to be in a state of "Return to Form" as it is fairly similar to how it was back in season 2, which I believe is probably caused from the backlash of the desert map.

In game store/loot- There are in game purchases for this game, mostly for the premium currency. Honestly, the currency is fairly cheep, and you can buy enough to get a battle pass for a whole season for about 10 bucks. The game also has another currency that you get for playing the game, ranking well, getting kills, winning etc, called coins. Coins can be used to purchase weapon skins/trinkets etc. which offers a f2p model for getting cool loot.(Although if you aren't consistently winning, farming up coins will most likely take a long time.) Otherwise, you're better off getting the battle pass, and maybe buying a few loot boxes.

Crashes/Glitches:
Throughout my time playing this game I have seen minimal issues regarding crashes/glitches. Currently, there seems to be an issue with the steam overlay being enabled, which may cause your game to crash randomly. I myself have the overlay disabled, and my game still seems to crash every once in a while. The only other gripes I have is that when jumping from high altitudes with the grappling hook, the game may stutter/glitch, and if this happens while you use your grappling hook, you will most likely die from fall damage.

I run this game at absolute maximum settings, and honestly I'd say besides COD, and maybe Apex, this game looks better than pretty much every other BR game I've ever played.

All in all, very solid game, if they marketed more, and fixed a few things, honestly it could be genre defining. There's a lot of good here, and a lot of questionable things as well, but I'll update this if anything big ever happens that I think deserves a review.

name: Portal
review:
Portal, developed by Valve and originally released in 2007 as part of The Orange Box collection, is a genre-defining first-person puzzle-platformer that remains one of the most innovative and tightly crafted games in modern gaming history. At first glance, Portal seems modest in scope—a brief, minimalist experience set in sterile testing chambers—but what it accomplishes in storytelling, gameplay design, and atmosphere with such brevity is nothing short of masterful. The game ingeniously blends mind-bending physics puzzles with a darkly comedic narrative, creating a timeless experience that challenges players intellectually while steadily building tension and intrigue through its deceptively simple premise.

The core mechanic of Portal—the ability to create two interconnected portals on surfaces and move instantaneously between them—completely redefined how players think about movement, space, and puzzle-solving in video games. This seemingly simple concept is explored with astonishing depth and elegance. Every chamber in the Aperture Science testing facility introduces a new idea or twist on the portal mechanic, escalating the challenge and requiring players to think creatively. The game avoids traditional combat or action in favor of spatial reasoning and momentum-based puzzles, making success feel genuinely earned through observation, logic, and experimentation.

From a gameplay standpoint, Portal is nearly flawless in its pacing and design. It introduces its mechanics gradually, never overwhelming the player, and then slowly raises the stakes. The difficulty curve is perfectly tuned, offering a satisfying sense of mastery without resorting to frustration. The player is never given a traditional tutorial—instead, the game teaches through doing, through experimentation and discovery. Valve’s mastery of environmental storytelling is on full display, with subtle changes in level design and presentation gradually revealing a much more sinister story beneath the surface.

That story unfolds through the ever-present voice of GLaDOS, the now-iconic AI antagonist who guides, mocks, and ultimately manipulates the player throughout the game. Voiced brilliantly by Ellen McLain, GLaDOS provides the game’s signature dry, passive-aggressive wit, which contrasts perfectly with the sterile and impersonal lab environments. Her sardonic humor, cryptic statements, and eventual breakdown are key to the game’s emotional arc. As players progress through what initially seem like simple puzzle chambers, they slowly uncover the implications of their situation—that they are not merely being tested, but imprisoned and watched in a crumbling facility. This narrative shift is subtle but powerful, transforming Portal from a clever puzzle game into a gripping escape story.

Visually, Portal leans into minimalism, but with purpose. The stark whites and grays of the testing chambers reinforce the feeling of isolation, sterility, and dehumanization, while occasional glimpses of decay, graffiti, or behind-the-scenes areas hint at a more complex and deteriorating world. The visual design serves both form and function—allowing players to focus on solving puzzles while also weaving an atmosphere of quiet unease. The game’s understated aesthetic holds up remarkably well even years later, thanks to its clean lines and clear visual language.

The audio design in Portal is equally meticulous. Ambient mechanical hums, subtle music cues, and GLaDOS’s voice work are all tightly integrated into the experience. The game’s final track, “Still Alive” by Jonathan Coulton, became an instant cult classic—a witty, haunting epilogue sung by GLaDOS herself that captures the game’s blend of dark humor and melancholy. It’s rare for a puzzle game to end with such emotional resonance, and Portal manages to deliver it without ever breaking the fourth wall too harshly.

Perhaps most remarkably, Portal manages to pack all of this—its innovation, its narrative subversion, its atmosphere—into a playtime of around 2–3 hours. While short by most standards, the experience feels perfectly measured. There’s no filler, no bloat. Every test chamber, every voice line, every environmental clue is purposeful. It’s a game that respects the player’s time while also providing a deeply memorable and thought-provoking journey.

If there is any criticism to be leveled at Portal, it is only that its brevity may leave some players wanting more—but this is quickly addressed by its equally excellent and more expansive sequel, Portal 2. Still, as a standalone experience, Portal is a near-perfect distillation of design efficiency and creative storytelling.

In conclusion, Portal is a landmark title that remains every bit as compelling today as it was at release. It is a rare example of a game that innovates not just in its mechanics, but in how it tells a story and engages the player intellectually and emotionally. Its iconic portal gun, deadpan humor, and unforgettable antagonist have earned it a permanent place in the gaming canon. For anyone interested in the intersection of gameplay design, narrative economy, and artistic elegance, Portal is not just recommended—it’s essential.

Rating: 9/10

One of Valve's cult-favorite classics, Portal is a puzzle game that tests your capabilities in many different ways.

The game hosts many different trial chambers that you must complete under specific scenarios. This may be getting a cube on a button, bouncing an energy orb to open a door, or using portals to traverse the room. With unique dangers like talking turrets that will shoot at you, witty dialog guiding you through the chambers, and the classic engine mechanics of Source, it is an all-around great time. There is also an added bonus of challenge chambers that test the player's capability of completing chambers using few portals, taking few steps, and making the shortest time.

While the game is not too long (compared to its sequel), Portal is all-around a good time if you need a fun little game to mess around with.

name: Don't Starve Together
review:
If Tim Burton directed a survival reality show and let the contestants slowly go insane, you'd get Don't Starve Together. This game doesn’t hold your hand—it slaps it, steals your food, and leaves you arguing with a talking flower while freezing to death.

I’ve spent 300+ hours trying (and hilariously failing) to survive. Whether it’s starving in winter because we forgot to plant enough carrots, or accidentally summoning Deerclops on Day 28 and watching our base turn into charcoal, every session is chaotic brilliance.

The hand-drawn art is timelessly eerie, the sound design is haunting yet whimsical, and the co-op experience… pure gold. But beware: it’s not for the faint of heart. If you rage-quit over burnt toast, this might not be your jam.

🪓 Pros: 
+ Rich, punishing survival mechanics
+ Unique characters with real personality
+ Mods add infinite variety
+ Every death is a story

💀 Cons: 
- Learning curve steeper than Wilson’s sanity drop
- Some updates leave old bugs kicking around like unwanted guests

Final verdict? DST is a beautiful, brutal fever dream—and I can’t stop waking up in it. 9/10, would eat monster lasagna again.

name: Don't Starve Together
review:
I usually love hard games to be clear. But I prefer them with a goal and end sight as a personal preference.

'Get experienced friends they make it fun' but I played with three of them and they went off doing whatever while I gathered wood and rock because, well, what else am I supposed to do? I can't spend time learning more in-depth mechanics because I'm getting attacked non-stop when I dare. I can't craft because the other's were prepping for fights and farming etc.. When I do dare and do get creative I am immediately slapped down for  the audacity, and not in a fun way that makes me want to repeat it. More a grumbling that I have to get everything I can before it's consumed by the wilderness. Without any tutorial that isn't me just flat out reading things online I don't actually know what anything is, or does.  Not a bad mechanic in theory but there's not much breathing room for a new player to engage and learn things, so I don't feel there's any other option available in-game. Combine that with some awful pathing, enemies movement being so quick they can't be clicked on in time, accidentally inspecting teammates because they came to help me causing even more deaths, and I wasn't really having a good time.

Hate the sound design playing the same cues over and over and over again. Thirty seconds pass? My strongman is weak again with the same sound cue. Have a small companion trailing you? Hope you LOVE Footsteps Audio playing nonstop in your ear at a oddly loud volume for not messing with any audio. That said all other music(ambient tracks and enemy cries, when not ganging up on me eight to one so it's overlapping sound bytes) are nice. The animations when they fire off are very fluid and the stylized art has a lot of love put into it.

The skill trees are nice but seem a little bloated in design.

Playing with others meant my internet, which is usually fine and yes I did check it, magically hit the rocks and did nothing. Constantly stuttering and randomly retreading ground. Slow animations constantly causing death, stuttered loops that made me re-click over and over frustrated out of my mind. Regular crashes and non-responsive in my whopping three hours of play. Call it a skill issue/clown award moment but it did pile on for me.

I did get experienced players to carry me after a bit that didn't click either. Doing busy work while they slowly got bored too, knowing the game and quickly overcoming early challenge with our base, then goofing around trying to hatch a bird egg just to see if they could before bouncing. I don't blame them. Other people love the game, and good for them! But I did not and won't recommend it.

Tips and tricks for the interested:

-If you're new just read online, get experienced friends to play with, or go on the easiest mode possible to wander and explore while you can

-Flower crowns are lovely for sanity

-Gather Flint immediately. Make an Axe, and Pickaxe. 

-Berries regrow so if you have the option, save any vegetables for emergencies and go for berries

-Crock Pot is great

SORROWFUL BE THE STARVING

If ur belly gnaws with the void of hunger
If ur sanity crumbles like stale breadcrumbs
If ur graveyard of worlds lies littered with the bones of Wilsons
Don’t Starve Together shall claim u, whispering: "Just one more night"

I, too, was once well-fed.
I, too, planted seeds with hope, danced with Beefalo,
and dared believe the darkness was my friend.
Yet here I kneel—a husk draped in Rabbit Ears,
my pockets full of Rot,
weirdly proud of my 17th demise-by-Goose.

🌑 THE UNHOLY TRINITY
Hunger

    A gnawing abyss.
    Berries mock you. Rabbits laugh as they dart.
    Your Crock Pot—a cursed altar—demands sacrifice:
    "Three twigs and a nightmare… for Meatballs?"
    This isn’t sustenance. It’s edible despair.

Darkness

    Charlie’s velvet claws.
    Shadows breathe. Fingers brush your neck.
    The lantern flickers—always as sanity snaps.
    You’ll huddle by the fire. You’ll weep for daylight.

Chaos

    The true deity.
    Deerclops at Day 29. Your base? Splinters.
    A "friendly" firefly ignites the forest.
    Your friend, starving, eats your last Pierogi.
    All is ash. All is beautiful.

☠️ SACRED SUFFERINGS (Highlights)

    *Permadeath: Watching your corpse decay as a ghost while friends ignore your woeful moans.

    *Winter: When hope freezes solid. (Also your toes.)

    *The Hounds: Hell’s doorbell. Always ringing when you’re naked and afraid.

    *Wortox: “I ate your soul. For healing. SORRYNOTSORRY.”

    *Caves: Where sanity goes to die… and depth worms throw the funeral.

⚰️ VERDICT

    10/10 WOULD STARVE AGAIN.
    This game didn’t just break me.
    It taught me the sacred geometry of panic-farming.
    It made me cherish the Goose that crushed my skull twelve times.
    It gifted me resilience (dubious), ingenuity (desperate),
    and an eternal craving for Monster Lasagna.

Now pardon me, Forsaken Ones.
The Nightmare Cycle approaches.
My Beefalo horn thirsts for another charge into oblivion.

Sorrowful be the stomach. Heavy be the log stack.
So Mote It Be. 🔥🪓

review:
Played both the main game and the DLC: The Following. 

The main game was super fun. There are multiple ways you can kill a zombie and so the combat is really satisfying. The parkour in the main game works so well, there are many buildings for you to climb and it's fun being able to kill zombies with parkour. Parkour mechanics are very satisfying as well.

Main game story was interesting, kind of predictable in some scenarios but overall a decent story.

The DLC: The Following wasn't as great as the main game because you are placed in the country side with not many buildings. You still do parkour but it's limited because you are in big fields most of the time. To get around the map, you use the Dune Buggy. The Dune Buggy is fun to drive though and you can add weapons and defence systems to it, which makes driving it even more fun.

But once you have completed the DLC: The Following, you realize the missions/quests/side quests all boil down to "go to point A, B, C, D, .... and collect X, Y, Z. You may argue that's most games. Sure but I wish there were more exploration missions/quests/side quests. Nevertheless, this isn't a big deal because at the end of the day, it's really fun to do the missions/quests/side quests as you have to get through a horde of zombies and you have to do that with combat. And as I said, combat in this game is really rewarding.

One con though is you can't play stealth in this game if you don't have a crossbow. The human enemies know exactly where you are if you get close to them, there is no way of sneaking up to them. You can sneak up to zombies though...

And this is not a con but it would have been cool if there was a sniper rifle added to the game or even a silencer, just to satisfy that itch of wanting to play stealthily for those who love playing that way.

The DLC: The Following is not a must. If you really enjoyed the main game, you will enjoy the DLC: The Following but not to the extent of the main game. It's not a Cyberpunk like DLC where it's a must play.

Other than that, I don't have anything bad to say about it, had heaps of fun.

name: Dying Light
review:
[h1]Dropkick and parkour your way through the zombie apocalypse![/h1]

[i]First-person action survival game set in a post-apocalyptic open world overrun by flesh-hungry zombies. Roam a city devastated by a mysterious virus epidemic. Scavenge for supplies, craft weapons, and face hordes of the infected.[/i]

[h2]Story & Quests[/h2]
You play as Kyle Crane, a GRE (Global Relief Effort) operative sent into Harran to recover sensitive data and assist survivors. But Crane quickly becomes entangled in the politics and morality of survival, forced to choose between duty and helping those in need.

[u]Story missions:[/u] Narratively driven, involving Crane’s role in the city’s fate.
[u]Side quests:[/u] Help survivors, clear quarantine zones, deliver drops.
[u]Random events:[/u] NPCs getting attacked, air drops landing, enemy ambushes.
[u]Safe zones:[/u] Areas you can clear and unlock to rest, store gear, and fast travel.

[h2]Gameplay[/h2]
Dying Light is a first-person action survival horror game, where killing zombies is the majority of the gameplay. Melee weapons are the primary means of attack, and consist of bats, crowbars, machetes, axes, swords - most are customizable. You can also attach weapon mods that add electricity, fire, or poison effects using crafting materials. You can collect materials to craft weapons, mods, traps, throwables, lockpicks, and healing items. Weapons degrade over time, forcing you to constantly scavenge and upgrade. Firearms are available as well, but rare early on, more common later. They're powerful but noisy (attract infected). You can also use a bow that is silent and deadly.

The parkour mechanic is another major part in this game and a really cool feature. You can climb, vault, and leap across rooftops and obstacles. You can climb almost anything - walls, ledges, rooftops, lamp posts, and more. As you level up, you gain parkour moves like dropkicks, wall runs, a grappling hook, and more. Dropkicking zombies is so satisfying. Movement feels fluid and is a big part of surviving. Movement is your lifeline, especially at night when fighting is often suicide. Being good at escaping is essential.

[u]The game features three major skill trees:[/u]
[b]Survivor[/b] – Crafting, better healing, shop discounts.
[b]Agility[/b] – Parkour moves, better stamina, mobility tricks.
[b]Power[/b] – Melee strength, finishing moves, combat efficiency.

You gain XP in each category based on what you do. Climbing boosts agility, fighting boosts power, etc. You also level up Crane’s gear: new blueprints, armor, and weapons.

The game can be played up to 4-player online co-op. It’s much more fun playing co-op than solo and it works really well.

[h2]Enemies & Bosses[/h2]
[u]The enemies and bosses consist of different zombies and humans:[/u]
[b]Biter[/b] - Basic zombie, slow.
[b]Viral[/b] - Faster zombie.
[b]Night Walker[/b] - Faster and more aggressive than Virals.
[b]Hazmat[/b] - Slow zombie with a gas tank on its back. 
[b]Goon[/b] - Large zombie wielding large melee weapons.
[b]Toad[/b] - Spit toxic acid from a distance.
[b]Screamer[/b] - Emit a loud scream when they see you, attracting Virals.
[b]Bomber[/b] - Bloated infected that run toward you and explode.
[b]Bolter[/b] - Flee immediately upon seeing you. Drop Bolter Tissue, used for crafting.
[b]Demolisher[/b] - Huge, tank-like infected with armor.
[b]Volatile[/b] - Ultra-aggressive night creatures.
[b]Rais' Men[/b] - Human bandits and thugs.

[h2]Environment[/h2]
The game takes place in Harran. It's an open world with a lot to do. The game has a dynamic day and night cycle. During daytime it's safer to explore, scavenge and complete missions as infected are slower and less aggressive. During nighttime zombies are more dangerous and Volatiles come out to hunt you. They are extremely fast and dangerous. You earn more XP for combat kills and agility moves. Missions become riskier but more rewarding.

The world is filled with activatable traps - car bombs, UV lights, environmental hazards - that can be used to kill zombies creatively. There are no invisible walls. If you can see it, you can probably get there.

[h2]Visual Design & Sound Design[/h2]
The game is beautifully designed. The city of Harran really looks apocalyptic. Corpses in the streets, graffiti on the walls, zombies everywhere. Harran feels like a real, decaying city under siege. The zombies and Volatiles look grotesque and intimidating. The infected don’t just look scary - they look diseased, like they’re falling apart. Melee effects are brutal where heads crack, limbs break, blood spurts.

The sound design is great. The Infected have different sound cues, which is important. Biters moan and gurgle constantly. Virals have panicked breathing or angry yelling before you see them. Volatiles have growls that are distinct and terrifying, with loud screeches when they spot you - immediate cue to run. They have heavy, thunderous footfalls - you can hear them sprinting up behind you.

Each weapon has unique sound effects: metal clanks, wood thuds, machete slashes. Hits sound crunchy and visceral - skulls crack, bones break, flesh tears.

[h2]Constructive Criticism[/h2]
While melee is the focus, gunplay is underwhelming. Weapons lack weight and aiming can feel stiff and unresponsive. Human enemies don’t offer challenging gunfights and are quite dumb many times.

Many side quests boil down to fetch quests or simple kill objectives. Boring and repetitive after a while.

The main story is formulaic and forgettable - a typical "undercover agent in a doomed city" arc. The villain Rais is generic and lacks depth - your standard violent tyrant with little motivation beyond cruelty. The final fight against Rais was a boring and annoying QTE.

[h2]The Verdict[/h2]
Dying Light is for sure one of the best co-op zombie-killing experiences out there. The melee combat is brutal and satisfying, the parkour is fun and immersive, and the world is beautiful. Despite the few flaws, Dying Light is a thrilling and addictive survival horror game that shines brightest when you’re running for your life, dropkicking zombies off rooftops, and barely escaping the night.

[h2]Rating: 9/10[/h2]

name: 7 Days to Die
review:
up until the most recent update, I would say, 7 days to die is my favorite survival game, for the reasons listed below. Positive review 1st, negative review 2nd

Positive review

1. Base building: When I think of this game the first thing that comes to mind is building a home, then building a massive horde base right after to survive the horde night. No other survival game I played left this good of an impression on me in this aspect. Base building is a learning curve but really fun once you get the hang of it if base building is your thing

2. Loot and Run: Going into poi's and trying to learn and study where the zombies would be and how I could save my friends some headaches, was really something that no other game I played managed to do, and I've played many loot and run games but 7dtd never got old for me in this aspect

3. Leveling up/skill sets: this is a bit of a partially positive and negative, because on one it can really liven up my game experience or completely ruin it. When progressing through the game and leveling up, sometimes I get really overpowered quickly or just stagnate for a painfully long time and suffer. In the classic game setting without storms and linear biome progression, usually looting in biomes I'm partially under-leveled for basically made my a worlds difference for my game. But that meant my worlds would last short because I got OP quickly, often times way too quickly (given the context I always play with zombies running and on insane difficulty) 

Negative Review
1: Linear biome progression, I tried this before they added the badges and the storms. It basically gutted the main thing I liked about this game, my home. Because of the quest progression you are probably gonna spend a very short amount of time in your biome unless you stagnate for a bit. So you don't really get time to spend two in games weeks building a home, because at most you will be building your horde base and have a bunch of boxes laying down near the trader, which kinda is a major decrease in quality of life. If linear biome progression and being locked by badges and I can't progress until I complete said badge quests, I don't want to play this game anymore. Because building boxes near a trader without a house is not the survival experience I find desirable.

2. Storms: it sounded like a good idea in concept. I really liked the idea of storms, I was kinda expecting like you get buffs by certain armors to protect you from the storm and certain food items kinda similar to the biome smoothies you take before the storm that give you brief protection or less damage in storm. Or even zombies specific to storms giving you a reason to be in the storm. But instead what we were given is a storm without any battling through it, kinda just you gotta hunker down in closed room or lose your health. I might as well just go outside IRL and touch grass, my friends can message me to get back on the game when the storm is done.

3: level caps, I honestly don't know the answer to this one, but with the biome badges, if you don't get the badges you feel like you are stagnant which I usually just restart from scratch with a new world when that happens. I basically throw what could be a really enjoyable run, because I feel like the badges are holding me back instead of enhancing my experience. And I want to experience the game to it's fullest but now I basically have to relearn the entire game, which I don't have the endurance for anymore.

I probably won't play this game until there is a rework on the storms and biome progression in a way that isn't just challenging for the sake of leveling up/grinding but for the sake of finding new ways to play and enjoy the game while having a challenge. There are so many ways to make the biome progression a really beautiful thing, I just don't think I can play this game and have fun until I see significant change in that aspect.

review: This might be the most disappointed I have ever been with an update for a game I enjoy. The 2.0 update has absolutely destroyed the freedom the player has to enjoy the game, forcing you to complete arbitrary and incredibly meticulous tasks to progress into other biomes with better loot. This by itself would not be a huge issue, if not for the loot you can find in each biome being hard capped in terms of its quality. This eliminates any reason to put down roots and build a base in the first couple of biomes, as it will just massively hinder you once you need better loot. I am incredibly confused as to why fun pimps thought this was a good idea. This game has had many many issues and changes regarding its progression and balance throughout the years, but most of the previous changes at least encouraged players to explore or to utilize game mechanics instead of forcing them to migrate around the map and restricting player freedom. Instead of playing an open-world sandbox game where it is up to you to taker risks at more dangerous POIs, and slowly progress your loot quality as the hordes grow stronger, you are now forced into a constricting series of quests that you MUST do if you want to actually play the game and survive stronger hordes. It is absolutely mind-boggling that Fun Pimps would flip their game on its head and ruin the open-world zombie survival game they have been building for over 10 years. Seriously, why do the developers care so much about the way people play a game that is heavily focused co-op and PVE? The way you play the game and progress has become so micro-managed it's suffocating. Please, Fun Pimps, for the sake of this game, roll back this update, make major changes to it, or offer refunds for the player base that you have betrayed with this update.

review:
I love games in the Survival-Crafting Genre but I can't excuse the weird methodology that the Fun Pimps seem to have when it comes to updating the game.  Whether it's sporadically changing the flow of perk skill systems, completely redesigning loot tiers, or adding random features that overall seem to be implemented just for the sake of giving the player a hard time it's been harder and harder to support this game as it's life span continues on.

I'm going to be frank with it, this is NOT a $45 game, the fact that they even want to charge people that much on top of the high prices for DLC content post-launch is ridiculous.  This game has been out for roughly a decade now and all they have to show for it is a constant back and forth between changes they can't seem to solidify and that's just not typical for games in the genre.

Removing the ability to re-use glass jars, forcing you to use a progressive book tier system to unlock everything when the RNG is already so sporadic, the lack of variety in equipment, on top of the constant changes to the armor system that they seem to swap with every other build it just gets harder and harder to follow when you're out of the loop.

I've had my fun with this game surviving the horde nights, rushing to POIs to grab up as much loot as I can, fending off the screamers and the hordes that rush our bases, but even then that doesn't justify what ultimately makes up a jumbled mess of an experience.

Word of advice, if you WANT to play this game I would highly recommend waiting for a sale.  While I'm glad that this game has finally hit it's "Full Release" stage it really is at most like a $25 game.

Every biome that's not the Forest is now locked behind a sh!#y drink because of "environmental hazards" and yet your armour has no effect on resistances, what drugs were these devs on? Put this into perspective, After A21.2, all clothing customization is gone, all unique items like the ghillie suit, or hazmat is gone. Ahhh yes, 1.0 - Removed Hazmat Suit, 2.0 Added Lethal radiation that cannot be countered unless you drink a SMOOTHIE. Brilliant realism there you numbskulls, the hazmat suit was only in the game for like EVER.

I dont need to even mention DLC, idc if its just cosmetic, this game has been in ALPHA for like a DECADE, 1.0 just sort of recently released and these @$$hats have the audacity to ask for more money after they have nerfed, neutered, and removed many good features that were established and finished, if the updates were actually good, i wouldn't even question giving more money for DLC.

From gun models, to item quality changes to skill changes, the nail in the coffin was finding out that you need 381 skill points to max out, you know how much you used to need? like 260ish, why is this important? because the player maxes out at Level 300, or 304 skill points including the intro points meaning it is actually impossible to max out all your skills now, unless you get ULTRA lucky and wear the Nerd armour for the ENTIRE GAME, LVL 1 has a 5% chance for an extra point, LVL 2 is 10%, and LVL 6 is 50%

So let me get this even straighter, Your going to make clothing not mandatory for biomes, so that you may "broaden your playstyle" instead opting for $h!tty smoothies that last 5mins, and then seriously narrow your available playstyles down by REQUIRING the nerd armour to max out your skills. Did they even THINK about what they were doing? I don't think they even did the math on how many skills you needed. Which shows how much they playtest. As a long, long, LONG, time enjoyer of 7DTD through its rough and long history This did it, no more 2.0, no more 1.0, time to stay in 21.2 and mod the ever-loving crap out of the game, TFP you have genuinely, deeply, disappointed me. 

I have come to one conclusion, TFP hate any and all fun, you know why they got rid of what we loved? because we loved it. That's it that's all. I still recommend this game for those in the niche, but stay in 21.2, the newer updates don't even compare to how good the game USED to be.

A great game, I've got to say.

I wasn't expecting much from this game, but it turned out to be a pleasant surprise. It has some solid mechanics for its time, and while the story is short and has no continuity, it's still a lot of fun, it's got a lot of clever little parkour puzzles. Although I have to admit, I almost rage quit during some missions. My main complaint with the game is that enemies seem to track you through walls the spawn rate is pretty overkill and enemies you've already killed will oftentimes respawn in cleared areas during certain mission phases. Plus you always have to be careful with your ammo because it runs out very fast often leaving you with just your secondary weapon(if you're lucky) or even your knife.

Overall, it's a great game and a solid Counter Strike story mode if you ask me. Too bad it got lost in the shuffle and never got the attention it deserved.

name: Counter-Strike: Condition Zero
review:
Note: This review is primarily about the deleted scenes portion of the game, which if you're here its most likely because you heard CS:CZ was a campaign mode entry into the series. That part is Counter Strike: Condition Zero Deleted Scenes which comes with the main game (which is basically just 1.6 with fairly impressive ai for the time), Its the one you would want to play however I wouldn't really recommend it. 

On paper it seems dope, but maaaan does it have a lot of stuff holding it back. To start the game is just fragmented missions. No connecting story line at all. You are given an world map and take the role of different spec ops teams from around the globe (even Russia which is interesting to see them portrayed as good guys from a western developer). You never play as the terrorists which sucks since its half of CS' identity. 

Since you aren't here for the story, is the gameplay and level design any good at least? Ehhhhh... while the game is built on source, an engine dear to my heart and one renowned for its interesting physics. It has been completely gutted here, patching out fun mechanics like bhopping making the boring level design even more prominent. Did I mention the levels completely blow? Ok that's not all true, some are really interesting! Pretty much every level designed by Russell Meakim has an interesting setting combined with a good selection of weapons. However even these fall victim to some noticeable design flaws. I played all levels at max difficulty, which revealed how poorly placed enemies can be. Sometimes they mimic real CS being tucked in tight corners that you have to clear on entries. This is fine however often they can be placed at the start and ends of ladders and climbing objects. If you've ever played CS you'd know this is fucked up. So whenever I got on a ladder I would get one-tapped (due to high difficulty) with no way to defend myself. My skills aren't being tested here, just my patience.

Anyways some are worth playing some are pretty bad filler, if you're super curious I'd say give it a go. If anything atleast you get the wildest credit scene to send you out. 

Oh and also Ig its a product of the time but this game fetishizes asian women quite a bit so.. yeah

4/10

name: eFootball
review:
This is obviously the worst PES game I've ever played. But it shows that Konami wants to get away from the recycle-old-game-and-stick-a-new-name-on scheme. Some ideas and approaches are very good (more movements without the ball, cross-play, transitionless corners and throw-ins, etc...), but the implementation is very miserable. To be honest, even old functions that have always worked flawlessly are miserable now. In the end, this just shows how hard it actually is to bring a completely new game to market instead of remarketing the same game for full price. I like the approach of putting more effort into the football games, bringing new features and taking risks. It's a shame that PES flopped this year, but since it's free, you shouldn't bitch so much. Kudos to Konami for daring to make this right step. I'll wait for EFootball until it's ready.

Edit.

The updated version of EFootball is not comparable to the beta version which was very criticized. The game runs very smoothly and I hardly had any bugs, the graphics and animations look very realistic especially on high graphics settings. The game dynamics are rarely disturbed by fading to freekicks or throw-ins, the game continues to run while the players are getting the ball ready, which is very good. When there are cut scenes they are well used and hardly interfere. It feels more like watching a game on TV.
The game dynamics have also improved a lot, offensive players move smartly and the defense also makes few mistakes. In order to get a goal situation you have to either trick the opponent to open up passing situations or outplay the opponent with well-directed passes. At the moment, besides the friendly matches and online games, there is only the Dream Team mode, where you create and manage a team online and play against the AI or online games. It is good that you can buy the standard players directly and do not have to pull from "packs". These then start at level 0 and you have to level them up to their normal value and then you can go a bit beyond that. Very good I found here the possibility that you can choose the value upgrades yourself and thus can form your perfect player. You can e.g. skill MBappe to be more focused on speed and dribbling to let him play more on the wing or increase the values for finishing and attacking to set him up as a center forward. The choice is up to you. Since Efootball is free, there is a fear that the game will become pay-to-win. So far, however, I have been able to do well with my non-pay-to-win team and have not had the feeling that I had a big disadvantage compared to the other players. The good thing is that Featured players and the "normal form" of the same players usually have the same values when they are at the highest level. Featured players just start at a higher value and don't need to level up as long. Also, Featured players often have an alternate focus on skills. Only some legend players that are hard to get are a lot better than the "normal" counterparts. I would have been happy if legendaries had been just as good and you only acquired them, for example, if you were a big fan, so as not to break the balance of the game. But so far opponents had only 2-3 legends in the team and the difference was not so big that you have no chance against them.

All in all, I think the game is good, it's fun and brings a lot of new features. But some corners must still be tweaked.

review:
WARNING: DO NOT WASTE A SINGLE CENT ON THIS GAME. Let it resolve its issues (current version is v0.9, so...) and come check after a while. Perhaps on black friday... If you don't play online, stick with 2021 and install a mod.

Now, on to more detailed feedback. Veteran since PES 3 with Collina on the cover, so I skipped the first match because the game wasn't allowing me to change the control settings. With that problem solved on the main menu, I played two games. One online, then one offline. No issue online, took a bit to find to an opponent but I think is rather normal at this time... 
It is a TOTAL revamp. You really can't even identify anything from eFootball PES 2021. Playability is rather realistic, in an awful way. I simply hate it. It’s no FIFA, but it’s not good either. The player drifts like crazy and controlling the ball gets more complicated each year, needs more and more input. You either use like five fingers to make it do what you want or you loosing control of the ball is a rather realistic result. Tacking and pressuring also seems to be getting hard by the year and it achieved another level with this game. 

Menus are completely different and a bit confusing, but with some extra features. Still, its presentation is very basic, hopefully with more game features coming out, that will improve. Training, on the other hand, went from a full feature to a video… Gosh! -_-‘

It really feels like a new game from scratch, thus the number of bugs already identified. KONAMI should paid some of the money back. They just released the game and that's it. I paid 40€ for this premium thing, and yet it feels like I'm apart of some sort of beta testing... Honestly, what a waist of (my) money.

In short:
The first release was still too early in my opinion. Though the roadmap, which has been public for a while now, does clearly state that some of the main content will be provided as updates until early next year. 
Beside this and a few flaws here and there, it is fun to play. Physics and flow etc. are already much better than in comparable games (e.g. F..A). Though there is still room for improvement. As there has been in PES in the past. 
In the end a no-brainer for me.

For all players with negative reviews:
Check your graphics settings in game! 
I have no problem with 4K@120, it's running buttery smooth (RTX 3090).
Since the engine changed, there are many graphics options compared to the past versions.
If your graphics card does not provide enough power, it can be stuttery as hell.

review:
So, this project started out as a 3D version of the successful game "Hooligansgame" made by a Polish company in Łódź, who were also known to release "Ultras Online" back in the day. The developers of THIS game wanted to piggyback off their success but became a sad attempt after all, starting out under the name of "Hooligan fighters", later "Hooligan Warriors" naturally the people expected the developers to add actual club insignia and perhaps an overworld. When the developers realized it was too much work, they gave up on the concept, made it a generic fighting game and renamed it "Street Warriors online", which already in itself tells you how much they care about their fanbased compared to how much they only care about a quick buck.

While they did put some effort in motion tracking to make the fighting moves realistic and while the maps are beautifully designed I really, really urge you not to play this game due to the developer's crappy mentality that only goes after money, unwilling to listen to any feedback the users give them. Believe me, I gave them a shot, I tried to make them listen but to no avail. The fighting in itself is really generic, stale and requires no skills at all. And instead of doing something about it, the developers, yet again, fail to listen to constructive criticism and instead make a salty post on Facebook simply calling everyone a hater and begging people for thumbs up.

name: Z1 Battle Royale
review:
Rating: 4/10

Z1 Battle Royale (formerly H1Z1) was once the king of battle royale games, inspiring the entire genre before games like PUBG, Fortnite, and Apex Legends took over. Released as H1Z1 in 2015, it had a fast-paced, arcade-style approach to battle royale, with fun gunplay, intense fights, and smooth vehicle mechanics. However, due to developer mismanagement, failed updates, and a declining player base, the game lost its identity and never fully recovered.

What Made It Great? (Back in the Day)
🔫 Fast-Paced, Fun Gunplay
Unlike PUBG’s realistic shooting, Z1 Battle Royale had a more arcade-like combat system, where movement, aim, and positioning mattered most. The snappy gunplay and quick fights made for a highly competitive experience, attracting many hardcore players.

🚗 Awesome Vehicle Combat
Z1 introduced cars and driving mechanics that felt smooth and responsive, making chases and escapes some of the most exciting moments in battle royale history. The introduction of police cars, jeeps, and off-road vehicles added depth to gameplay.

🏆 One of the First Battle Royale Games
Long before PUBG and Fortnite, H1Z1 pioneered the last-man-standing formula. It was a Twitch favorite in its prime, with huge tournaments and a thriving esports scene.

🤝 Strong Competitive Scene (For a While)
At its peak, H1Z1 Pro League had top esports teams and players competing in high-stakes matches. It was one of the first battle royales to feature ranked matchmaking and skill-based leaderboards.

What Went Wrong?
❌ Too Many Bad Updates
The developers made drastic changes to the gameplay that alienated the core player base. Updates ruined the gun mechanics, movement, and vehicle handling, turning a once-loved game into a frustrating mess.

❌ Name Changes and Identity Crisis
The game went through too many rebrands:

H1Z1: King of the Kill
H1Z1
Z1 Battle Royale
Each version tried to "fix" the game, but instead, it lost players and direction with every update.
❌ Player Base Collapse
At its peak, H1Z1 had over 100,000 concurrent players. Now, finding a match is nearly impossible due to the drastic decline in population. Most players have moved on to PUBG, Fortnite, or Warzone.

❌ Competitors Did It Better
When PUBG came out, it offered better gunplay and realism. When Fortnite launched, it brought fun building mechanics and a casual-friendly style. Z1 Battle Royale failed to keep up, and players abandoned it for better alternatives.

Conclusion
Once a trailblazer in battle royale gaming, Z1 Battle Royale (H1Z1) has now become a ghost town, abandoned due to bad updates, poor decisions, and stronger competition. While it deserves credit for inspiring the genre, it’s hard to recommend in 2025, as matches are difficult to find, and the gameplay is not what it once was.

Rating: 4/10 – A battle royale pioneer that lost its way. Play only for nostalgia, but don’t expect much.

review:
Playtime: 1200 hours
TL;DR: Sadly, I can’t recommend this game to anyone right now.

Pros

•	Atmospheric
•	Crisp sound design
•	Beautiful graphics
•	Unique, niche experience

Cons

1. Terrible UI
•	Since the engine upgrade, the UI has taken a massive hit. It's clunky, unintuitive, and nowhere near what could be considered even "decent."
•	While it's slowly improving with each update, it's still far from acceptable.

2. Questionable balancing decisions
•	The game heavily rewards passive or “rat” gameplay, actively discouraging aggression.
o	Example: Nerfing wall penetration makes it easier for players to camp inside buildings.
o	Releasing and buffing silenced weapons.
o	Repeated buffs to traps.
o	Nerfs to stamina, poison resistance, and regeneration shots.

3. Performance issues
•	The beautiful graphics come at a cost: noticeable micro-stutters even on high-end systems.
•	A known issue causes VRAM not to unload properly, leading to decreasing FPS the longer you're in a session. The only 
        fix is restarting the game.

4. Broken matchmaking
•	The matchmaking system is completely unbalanced. The 6-star MMR bracket is so wide that I often get matched against players with double or even triple my playtime—especially frustrating as a solo player.
•	No ping limit: Many 6-star lobbies are filled with Chinese and Russian players abusing high ping on EU servers.


I genuinely want to recommend this game, but in its current state—I just can’t.

name: Hunt: Showdown 1896
review:
Like many players, I took a hiatus from this wonderful game when the 1896 update flopped, and I was reluctant to come back. I logged back in a handful of times hoping that the game would at the least function properly and it seems that through all the tribulations this game has gone through, the devs finally got it to a stable state to build on, which is ironic given the judgement of the fool launch mishap. I've been playing it a lot the past couple of weeks and I've been having just as much fun as I did when I started playing pre-1896, which is extremely refreshing. The game isn't perfect by any means, but it's no longer frustratingly broken and actually runs better on my PC than it ever has before. 

If you're new, ignore the reviews about the UI and the 1896 doomsdayers. If you never played OG Hunt, the UI being changed won't be meaningful to you at all. After reminiscing about the old UI through videos and just from taking a long break from the game, I've actually changed my own mind and I think the devs were right and the new UI actually IS better than the old one. Perfect? No. Improved? Yes.

The other problem with the 1896 update was the removal of all the old maps and the atrocious issues with servers and technical performance, which led to the reviews falling to mixed. The old maps are back and the game definitely runs smoother than it ever has, so all of those old reviews are moot now. 

This is the first time I've been compelled to write a game review and I just want as many people to know that while definitely far from perfect, the game is enjoyable and on the upswing. If you need a sign to grab the game and hop in, this is it, especially while it's on sale. I purchased this game for many friends when I initially got into it and this is the first time it's been back to the point that I would do so again.

If you're an old player, now's the time to jump back in. If you're a new player, now's the time to dive in headfirst. See ya'll in the Bayou and enjoy the Hunt.

name: Hunt: Showdown 1896
review:
A bit of a dated review, but when I initially played the game, it was (and continues to be) a very unique approach to PvPvE. While there may be things that could feel old within the game with the current mechanics, there are aspects of it that are fantastic and, after a while, you wish were in other online games. One of such things is the fact that *everything* makes a noise in this game. The only way you can't make any noise is by standing still and doing absolutely nothing. There are ways (if you progress with a particular character aka hunter) to reduce/nullify the noise you make but you gotta make it alive before you can--otherwise you have to start over with that hunter.

The addition of the map in Colorado (with mountains, different environment/trees/views, and verticality), makes a great (relative) variety of maps. They aren't a lot of maps but you'll still spend a lot of time just trying to remember a lot of the different locations within each map as they've put a lot of effort into the design of each compund. The newly-upgraded DeSalle map is fantastic with an extra brush of color compared to the classic version and makes it feel newer.

Crytek continues to make updates to the game to tweak on certain things plus frequent events. I wish they'd sometimes take some liberty to be more experimental more often, but they try to tackle some high-priority feedback from the community as they can. I'm assuming they are a much smaller team right now compared to their top Crysis days, so they may not be able to move faster in terms of their roadmap. If you can get used to the aggressive learning curve at first, you may end up appreciating the unique elements of the game such as its weapons with tons of details with different properties and pros/cons, lower rate of fire, among other things such as a (potentially) slower approach to locations, playing the "hunting" game as you track down other players, the overall ambient sounds/atmosphere, etc. You have to have a good idea on how to approach the game and may be worthwhile looking up some entry-level tips by more experienced players beforehand, but this is a good game turned fantastic if you get to play with 1 or 2 other friends (you can play in 1-, 2-, or 3-player teams).

name: Hunt: Showdown 1896
review:
80% of my time with this game was in it's early access/first iterations. I know more people are pissed about recent changes, but i havn't even played the newest version of the game since they lost me awhile ago. This is was the last battle royale I bothered trying before really understanding they weren't for me.

The reason being is that this game does a lot of things really well, atmosphere and basic pve mechanics, the sound and hide and seek mechanics are a nice strategical layer to things, the gunplay is absolutely top notch. PVP (when I played at the time) was fair and solid, and not and overwhelming mess of needing meta knowledge of ammo types and builds.

Over time the game got needlessly complex. The UI wasn't updated when they started adding new currencies and tabs making it a cluttered mess to look at, much less navigate. Questionable design changes to systems that were solidly tested and enjoyed as far back as early access.. the devs just seem to have lost touch to me, and that was before this recent 1896 update.

I think this game sells itself on the idea very well.. and it's a great idea, implementing the hide and seek mechanics with the gunplay in this era. The moment to moment gameplay CAN be interesting when things unfold or do come together in those rare occasions where you've tracked that team and they ran into another team and you can set up a flank and get them both with yours.... but the reality is you will usually be creeping very slowly through maps to avoid sound traps or being seen. Lots of hiding, waiting, and educated guessing. You can play faster and more carelessly but even with a lot of knowledge it can work against you. Strategies are often based on movement, usually large flanks to force a mini encirclement, or to reposition outside the enemies incoming flank,  and spawn points will usually dictate the pace of your game. Spawning near another player spawn or early obj may totally change your approach to that game and put you more on "defense" than "offense" depending on how you choose to engage.

Simply put, I'm fine with the difficulty and learning curve in this game but I don't like how patience in this game doesn't always pay off,(even in a way where you learn something) the matches can be long, the updates can be rocky/questionable, and there's a lot of nothing going on a majority of your play time. The game doesn't respect my time enough for me to bother with it anymore, and I havn't even touched the game in years. Add to that the harshness of the character loss system, which, if I was learning a bit more of the why's and hows (like implementing an actual kill cam which the devs say they cannot do) i'd be more okay with, but after putting so much time into a character only to have no idea where I went wrong - what sight line was I accidentally in, what was the sound I made that pulled their attention - did they just stumble into me? Things like this are never really answered so i just have to guess how to change my gameplan on the next go round with a crappier character.

A game on Hunt Runs for 45 minutes, you can extract early, but an early game is still about 15-20min. 80%-90% of that time will be waiting or looking to take a shot. This "lots of nothing for a minute of something" seems to be a Royale problem inherently, which is what I meant earlier, the game does what it does very well, It's just catering more to that hardcore punishing type of royale MP gamer more over time and that's just not my speed. Something like this on a smaller map, maybe round based with lives is more my thing. Great start to the idea though.
