review:
I mean, I love this game so Ill give it a reccomended but its far from perfect, VERY FAR.

From me sucking being a complaint to the games hit registration being questionable, I have quite a few problems. If you've perused the reviews at all, I assume two things will appear the most; UI issues, and the review bombing of updating issues. UI issues definitely exist, but to be honest I'm new enough to not know anything else other than general UI complaints. The loadout menu is a nightmare but thats my onlly real complaint with the UI, the rest is manageable.
The update issues are also very real, with every major update for an event the servers seem to, without fail, die. It sucks for those of us who are super hyped to play the new update but we get it eventually and SOME form of compensation, so I don't mind TOO much. Other games are no better- well that's not entirely true. For the most recent event--judgement of the fool--the servers were down for an ungodly amount of time and then the update was rolled back for a while. I don't intend to hate on OR glaze crytek, theyre a company that delivered my favorite game that I've spent SO MUCH money on.

The actual game, disregarding problems is like nothing I've ever played before. Extraction shooters tend to all feel the same, this one was incredibly addictive but also incredibly unforgiving. One or two shots and you've died, now, to be fair, the guns are slow to rechamber but a single headshot from any gun will end your entire run early. Peek a corner one time too many as a solo, already used your revive trait(Excusively for solo players) welp, there goes your run. Its addictive, and has good enough balancing to not make anything feel unfair at all. You can go into a fight with the most expensive weapons and a full collection of traits and die just as easy as if you had nothing. 

In short, its addicted me with about 300 hours between PC and PS5, and I would feel bad to give it any less than a recommendation on steam. Give it a go if it's on sale, wait for a sale if it's not. It'll be completely unique, but whether that uniqueness is good or bad is up to you.

name: Sekiro: Shadows Die Twice - GOTY Edition
review:
[h1]Sekiro: A category of its own[/h1]
When I first started this game, I really wasn't feeling it. Having played many other games with heavy parry mechanics, I just didn't understand why every enemy kept blocking my attacks, and waiting to parry every enemy for counterattacks felt very tedious. It also didn't help that just about every section of the map was packed with enemies that would swarm me as soon as one got alerted to my presence. I didn't find the game "hard" per se; I beat every one of the early bosses I encountered on the first try, but I found the overall gameplay very tedious.

I was about to call it quits, until I beat a certain [spoiler]Genichiro[/spoiler] boss, that I finally understood the game and its core combat mechanic: posture.

See, what got me confused is that Sekiro kept getting described as a "parry game". And while parrying is somewhat of an important mechanic in this game, Sekiro should be more accurately described as an "aggression game". This is because that unlike other parry focused games out there, Sekiro isn't really about the patient dance of parrying and counterattacking.
Really, it's more about hacking away at enemies and consistently applying pressure due to the posture mechanic. Because guess what, it doesn't matter if your enemies block your attacks; your goal for 95% of encounters is to overwhelm your enemies with enough attacks to allow you to land that insta-kill deathblow.

And it is AMAZING how much you can get away with by simply tapping the attack button. Oh no, you opponent is about to hit you with an unblockable attack? Well, just thwack them in the face with your sword and they get interrupted (disclaimer: does not work every time). It was pretty funny realising that instead of waiting for enemies to attack, I could simply continuously attack, parry counterattacks every 2-3 hits, and then just keep repeating the same process.

Also, dodging was often times a lot more efficient than parrying, because several bosses would straight up not finish their combo if you dodged to get behind them. This is most obvious with the much hated [spoiler]Demon of Hatred[/spoiler] boss, which is trivialised by merely getting behind him, and jumping every now and then.

The second most important thing that I learned the hard way, was just how much [b]stealth[/b] is important in this game. Sekiro absolutely SUCKS at dealing with more than one enemy at a time; it doesn't even matter what sort of grunt you're dealing with- face more than one enemy at a time and you end up dying very quickly. 
So once I actually started playing like a ninja- crouching and luring away enemies for backstabs, exploring the world became a lot more tolerable and even enjoyable.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
Can take awhile to get used to, but once the posture mechanic "clicks", along with adopting a stealth approach to exploration, Sekiro can become a very satisfying experience. [b]9/10[/b] ([i]-1 for the camera boss[/i])

review: This game is exactly what i've been looking for in a twin stick shooter and IMO succeeds where so many others in this genre have failed. Build crafting is really fun and offers a lot of room for customization based on the play style you want. Want to make a bad*** laser sword dude that zips around the map and cutting enemies to pieces? Cybercorps got it. Want to play with turrets/drones and watch enemies health bars drop as they enter your kill zones? Cybercorps got it. The game constantly rewards you with useful loot and the perks/card system is solid once you understand how it works. Story is decent (if not a little talky) but the game nails the cyberpunk theme which i love. I've only played levels on normal so far but combat encounters are challenging, fun, and reward perfect reloads/dodges. I haven't even touched multiplayer yet, but I imagine that would be a ton of fun with 2 friends with everyone bringing their wild builds into the fights together. I haven't experienced any bugs yet and the game runs great on my 5+ yr old machine. Highly recommend for fans of games like this.

name: CyberCorp
review:
Cant recommend personally. The gunplay feels like a water gun fight, I'd say nerf, but I think even nerf guns have too much oomph to be comparable. Melee is fun enough but the formula of "hit a guy a few times then smack the execution button" gets old pretty fast. The story and dialogue are both also completely inept, uninteresting and full of typos which I assume are the result of a lazy translation. I could ignore story/dialogue and focus on the tight and satisfying gameplay IF the gameplay were either tight or satisfying. Similarly if the characters and story were interestingly written, I could push through the lackluster gameplay to follow along. CyberCorp misses on both. 
To be honest CyberCorp didn't even hold my attention for an hour, after the first 3 or so missions I couldn't help but feel like I was wasting my time. 

Similar games that I personally enjoy much more: 
-The Ascent (similar cyberpunk setting and rpg elements, but with great combat and an engaging plot. The Ascent also makes MUCH better use of said cyberpunk setting)
-RUINER (less focus on story/exploration than The Ascent but with even tighter, more precise gameplay in a cyberpunk setting) 
-Synthetik (Not a cyberpunk setting but has a similar retrofuturistic aesthetic, twin stick roguelike with some of THE most satisfying  gunplay i've experienced)

name: CyberCorp
review:
Very fun looter shooter with a lot of potential. While I think the game has some issues especially at the end game and fall for the same traps almost every game in the genre has the positives overall outweigh the negatives and after finishing the story missions I wanted more so that's a thumbs up from me. For the asking price it's a steal.

------

[b] I am going to talk my issues with the end game below that I believe can be addressed with some minor tweaks: [/b]
1- Enemy types: Humans are fine and challenging enough. Robot enemies on the other hand are not, some robot types have way too much health/shields for their archetypes like kamikaze robots and melee spam robots. Enemies don't react to damage in this game so the these two types are especially annoying since they are going to rush you until the end.

2- Weapon variety: Shotguns and DMRs are kings in the end game. I tried other weapon types (not exotics tbf since you need to kill bosses to get them as far as I know) but they are just not effective enough. Again, because the fact enemies don't flinch to damage burst damage is always better than sustained damage. Rocket launchers are great until you realize self explosion damage is a thing lol.

3- Endgame map variety: Randomly generated missions use preset maps and they get old quickly, Story missions maps are surprisingly well done with some hidden secrets sprinkled around and fun to play. However, random missions maps presets are very few and get old quickly unfortunately, I suggest raising the reward level for story missions to the maximum (60) after the player hits power level 55.

Obviously a lot more can be done but I understand that indie developers don't have the time or the budget to push major changes.

name: CyberCorp
review: CyberCorp is an isometric twin-stick shooter. As you can guess from the name, the game takes place in a cyberpunk world. You fight against robots, thugs with implants, and mechs to stop an evil corporation from mind-controlling people with their new chip. If you have played a looter shooter like Borderlands or Destiny before, you already know what you're getting into. The core gameplay revolves around finishing missions and getting new weapons and armor. Then you complete the same mission with increased difficulty for better loot. Rinse and repeat. In between missions you are in your safehouse, which acts as a HUB. You can upgrade your gear, watch TV, or buy new stuff from the shop while in the safehouse. The gameplay is excellent in CyberCorp. It's fast-paced and rewarding. The game encourages an aggressive playstyle. Especially melee combat is really satisfying. Customization is amazing. You can customize everything in the game. Visuals and the color of your armor or the color of your weapon. Variety is superb, and you can create cool-looking characters. The game is very short, unfortunately. If you don't grind or don't do any of the side missions, you can easily beat it in a day. Optimization is fine for the most part, but there are some frame drops here and there. The music is average, nothing special about it. Overall, CyberCorp is a great game. If you like this genre, I'm sure you'll like CyberCorp

name: CyberCorp
review:
I came across this game via a Reddit post from the developer himself and it looked neat enough to pick up.
Dear Dev, if you see this, I am not trying to be rude or hurt your feelings, just want to provide my opinions!!

It's not bad, and has potential, but I am a bit disappointing, I do think this could have cooked a bit longer.
Integrally speaking i think it has a good game idea.

My Criticisms:
-Sound design is bad, its not cohesive, very tinny overall, impacts and guns feel pathetic, music doesn't sound fitting and isn't mixed very well.
-Clunky game feel, many animations feel simply too slow to be useful, like the sword F kills. 
-Movement feels slippery and heavy at the same time. 
-And combat just has no impact, maybe a game slowdown on impact or more clear visual effects/knock-back could help(sound design too).
-Starting the game in the lobby was an odd choice, as well as having the level you select being the intro screen, it just felt disorganized. 
-UI for equipment uses full new tabs to manage stuff but could benefit from popup menus more to make going around easier.
-Map design, at least in the first level was wayyyy too linear, this can hurt a looter shooter especially if linear story progression is in place, as leveling up items becomes more of a best number game rather than exploration and freedom.
-Art style is not cohesive at all, and the low-poly look can work, but the overdone visual effects combined with this mismatched blurry environment is just an odd clash.
-The writing is rough, its conceptually there but very rough.
-That's all I can think of at the moment haha!

Overall:
It's just not FUN to play yet, the concept is sound, and the overall idea and aesthetic make sense, but its under-baked for the time being, It's definitely more in a Early Access state still. I'm refunding the game for now in hope some of these changes get implemented and I can pick it back up later!

Side quests are also significantly harder then the main missions of what unlocks. 

There is also some serious stability issues. 
Constantly falling through floors, getting stuck in walls, trouble walking up stairs, and the game keeps forgetting what difficulty it's on. My personal favorite is when one player can walk through a door and the other can't. Or even better when the game "Hiccups" and one player gets randomly teleported halfway through the level.

For example, I loaded up a Lv24 difficulty mission. It went form "okay" to bullet sponge central. It was absolutely not the difficulty of a lv24 run. 
After grinding through the boss, I ended up getting nearly a full set of lv 32 gear. My coop partner? He got lv 26 loot. 

The game keeps bouncing between too easy and dying in one hit, with very little in between. 

Even the Unstick button doesn't work. I've "loaded" into what I believe was the floor a few times, and the unstick button just moves my position slightly, and that's it. We still have to reload a few times. 

Considering I'm only about 4 hours into the game, and I've had to restart maps roughly 20% of the time due to extreme glitches, that's not exactly a good ratio.

name: CyberCorp
review:
This top-down shooter ARPG (not a roguelite) had a fair bit of fun potential, but flopped out of early access like a fish gasping for air in the boat, with bugs and a suspicious smell as though the early access time was shortened from a year to a mere eight months.  Ever see a game come out four months early because it was just in that great of shape?  Not here either, and there are issues reported years before early access even started when it was just a demo.  Expect plenty of jank and clunky action and you might have an ok time, but the game does feel rather limited, and the higher difficulty seems, well, very [i]annoying[/i] on top of those limitations.

There are only a few fairly set missions to play over and over, with fifteen mainline story missions plus about six types of "side" missions, but the bigger issue is the game basically only knows one trick: spawn constant stream of enemies in walled area until done.  There's no endgame, just replaying the same few missions hoping for new drops (which are set by mission and viewable, so you may not even have choices for where you go if you want something specific, but at least you can see that in-game) and combining upgrades to push them up tiers.  This leaves a lot of grinding and general sameyness in place of content or interesting things to actually do.

And sameyness is an issue.  The game throws a lot of enemies at you, and has a surprising library of really annoying enemies, from guys that charge a sweeping slide which can down you from off screen, large AoE stomps that drop with no warning, snipers that vanish as you hit them, annoying beam bots that track you about as fast as you move, and let's not forget one of the greatest action sins ever conceived: attacks that reverse the player's controls.  Yet, despite enemy diversity, how the fights run blurs a lot of specifics together and leaves you more frantically wearing down local annoyances than enjoying the dance of battle.  You are driven around like a kite on the wind by the mass of incoming damage/powers that feel more like relentless pestering, and you often cannot just focus down specific targets (especially troublesome when some have large regenerating shields) and just feel no real control of the field.  So often, games take us from technological supersoldier to child running around table.

In gearing, it costs special currency to apply upgrades, to remove/replace upgrades, [i]and[/i] to combine upgrades, so that special currency really obstructs you and feels like merely another grind element in place of content value.  I don't really find drop rates and currency sandbags "content", but if you have a high tolerance for that, it might feel like less of a drag, but it's definitely still a drag, and you can't just swap your build around to play differently or try out a new item, because gear changes get so expensive and combining mods to climb tiers makes it that much harder to actually have spares of things (on top of ballooning costs).  Drops already hold you back plenty, so the added special currency sandbag to even swapping mods just feels unnecessary and anti-player.  And then you get to the special-tier "exotic" gear, which comes with all its slots locked so you cannot change anything, and just get whatever random variation of affixes and cards it drops with, instead of the whole upgrade custom system that's supposed to be adding value.  So, if you have your eye on one of those later, where stats matter more, you can only grind grind grind until it finally rolls a good drop.  It's a huge grind, on probably very few--if any--mission options, in a game with few options to begin with.  Especially when the game seems to have lifted not just the poor drop value (getting a good non-exotic you can use your fancy upgrades on is downright astronomical) and currency drag from toxic live service game models, but also the [i]requirement[/i] for boss grinding.  [i]Only[/i] the story boss missions drop gear with "endgame" tier affixes.  There are only [i]three(!)[/i] story boss fights in the game that can reward such gear, and not only do they get boring fast, there's gear that just doesn't drop there, so you can never get good versions of those items.  And when only three missions drop endgame valid loot, what even does endgame mean?  Once you're looking for endgame, anywhere else you go drops trash you don't want, and you can't even auto-break down loot.

Similarly, it does some downright strange things that feel simply way beyond the appropriate scope for the game, like daily login reward milestones, daily objective "quests", and achievements that require [i]hundreds[/i] of missions.  No one should putting on such mock live-service airs for a small indie shooter with 20 missions that are basically the same.  The game wants you to be tied to it and grind forever, but there's just no game here to do that with.

If you're wondering what exactly the play has, you have two guns, a melee weapon which may have a single fairly slow two or three hit combo, an invulnerable slide on cooldown (you can shoot or take other actions during the slide), and three slots for active abilities you pick from a pool of drops.  The game's design feels like it assumes you keep one of the quick-teleport movement abilities in your actives, so you may feel more like you have two dodges and two actually pickable actives.  Gun ammo is not limited, but you have clips with an active reload mechanism, so good timing can shorten your reload and contribute to your action combo (higher combo for action spaces gets some bonuses, so it's not just for show, but it's hard to pay any attention to either since fights are extremely busy).  Actives and slide all have pretty significant cooldowns, and actives both require drops and currency to upgrade.

Finally, I bought the game as early access opened in large part because of the cute Vanquish-esque slide actions you could do all over combat.  It kind of helped with the janky action and constant enemy pestering of attacks.  Shortly into early access, the slide was put on a problematic cooldown which basically killed that whole aspect of the combat feel, leaving the slide another clunky mechanic that doesn't quite fit or work.  The only consolation offered to that negative change was that you can sacrifice a significant amount of build space (and give up on exotic items in some gear slot(s), due to their upgrade lock-out) to stack multiple copies of upgrades that are one-per-mission 2% chance reward drops from a specific mission.  Frankly, I don't really feel like it's worth playing the game without that adjustment, and something like that really shouldn't take that level of grind and significant sacrificing of options to reinstate so the action makes sense again, but there's also no real reason a player would think to even do this nonsense, for how different more freely-usable sliding feels.  So, I'm mentioning this as a tip on how the action can change from its initial appearance, even though it certainly won't reach great.

Overall, I'm going to call it on the not recommend side, since most of the things I find important to say are warnings, and I feel like I'm more putting up with it to progress, than excited to spend time with it.  The price is pretty low, though, and the co-op seems to [i]mostly[/i] function playably ([i]finally[/i]--co-op was a terrible mess for the entirety of early access), so that might earn it some time regardless, as the co-op top-down shooter ARPG space is pretty nonexistant, but co-op requires one or two more people willing to put up with it for you.  My co-op partner would rather play other games that are more fun, and I don't blame them.

Honestly, this whole review could just say, "Frequently reverses player controls during movement-critical fights, even bosses."  That's trying to really earn that thumbs down, even without counting the buggy and unobtainable achievements or three-mission endgame.

- Blinking in the direction of movement makes sense for controller, but on mouse & keyboard I'd have hoped it to be in the direction of my cursor, or at least have an option to toggle it so.
- Inconsistent depictions of the loot table, an exotic item may be displayed with a set of rolls but do not always spawn with them. If it's meant to be fixed rolls, ensure it; if it's not meant to be fixed rolls, don't show any when displaying the item.

- good "shell" (robot) customization
- decent mission variety
- very good enemy variety
- good price
----------------------------------
Negatives:
- The main Story is nothing special and is overall pretty short that end on a cliff hanger (6-10hrs depending on your build and if you do side missions)

- Still some janky aspects even after EA, like getting soft locked due to buggy mission triggers, luckily the game does have a built in "unstuck" button that can get you out of most bugs I have ran into.

- I bought the game day one of EA and I'm kind of disappointed that no new main missions have been added since release. I understand this is a smaller indie game but I as left wanting more main mission variety and it kind of abruptly ends leaving the player the ability to go and grind their character up to max level and redoing the missions on the hardest difficulties.

- Depending on who you are this may be a positive or negative but from my experience M/KB feels much better then controller.
------------------------------------
Final Thoughts:

If you like looter shooters and want something more bit sized then the usual live service crap that fills this genre, this game may be for you. I can 100% recommend it for its current price tag as even if the main story is short there is still tons of side content to grind to min max your character.

name: CyberCorp
review:
Alien Shooter in Cyberpunk Style

I should note that the game officially released on April 22, and as of the time of writing this text—April 24—only two days have passed, so it's understandable that bugs and issues are inevitable. However, their number is  large.

As strange as it may sound, before I start criticizing the game, I want to mention that I liked its concept and how it is supposed to be played. I believe that once it is polished, it will be enjoyable. But right now, it's a mediocre title that will only appeal to fans of Alien Shooter and CyberPunk.

Let me start with the positives: the game has decent visuals and is optimized compared to many other games currently being released. There is a variety of weapons and skills, as well as the option to play cooperatively.

The game lacks voice acting—at least in English. It's clear that the developers intended to add voice acting, but so far it only exists for enemies, and not all of them at that.

In the game, you can use three types of weapons: melee, primary, and secondary. You can experiment with weapons—changing them during missions. However, the shooting feel is poor: whether you're shooting a pistol, shotgun, or submachine gun, there isn't much difference; only the model and tracers vary.

Now about skills: out of all the skills available, only a few make sense to use—namely blink and turret. My friend and I (we played both solo and cooperatively) didn't use anything else—and there was no need to. Blink is necessary for quickly closing in on an enemy or escaping from one. The turret deals some damage and distracts all enemies towards itself, allowing you to recover some health and armor. Various shields, zones, grenades, and mines are unnecessary—they're just there for variety without enhancing gameplay.

Regarding missions: locations either repeat visually or in level design. You can also often notice texture issues—they start overlapping each other or disappearing from certain angles.

At the beginning, I mentioned that the game resembles Alien Shooter in a cyberpunk style. In Alien Shooter, mobs appeared from holes in walls or floors; if they appeared differently—there was some effect. Here you can kill a boss, and suddenly a mob appears out of thin air—WTF?

Continuing with mobs: during combat, it's not always clear whether a mob has a weapon or not; the only difference is in their name and weapon type. They all look completely identical; not even all mobs are recolored.

Regarding co-op: I specifically invited my friend along to avoid saying "These problems are only happening to you." No, these problems aren't just mine; some people notice them and some don't. Back to co-op: it's generally decent but has its downsides.

First: we were occasionally knocked aside.
Second: some missions are not well-optimized for co-op. For example, we couldn't enter a capture point location together; I had to complete it alone while my friend couldn't pass through a barrier. Damage could be dealt both to him and by him. 
Third: there aren't enough missions designed for co-op; I'd like something like an endless mode—as seen in Warframe—where after a certain time you can choose to finish the mission and collect resources or risk everything for increased rewards.

The sound design is good; it sets the pace in the game, so to speak. During fights, the music really comes into its own, and during shootouts, the tempo and volume of the music change, allowing you to fully immerse yourself in the world of cyberpunk. By the way, perhaps that's why in your apartment—which also serves as the game's hub—you can choose different soundtracks from the game and re-listen to your favorites. The music truly transports you to the world of cyberpunk, which has a very positive effect on your overall mood and attitude towards the game.

The game is being developed by 20 people and in fact, what they have done is not the worst product, the game has a right to exist, but it needs to be improved: add new missions; improve the usefulness of shields, grenades and mines; or reduce their number and improve the remaining elements; fix the errors with multiplayer.

Is the game raw? - YES; 
Did you like the game? - YES; 
Do I regret spending the money? - NO; 

Rating 5 out of 10

This game feels too clunky, and not in a "big gun: big damage" kind of clunky? I'm sure some people will know what I mean.

The dodging is a slide animation, and with a 2.5D top down perspective it sometimes just doesn't... feel like a dodge? It's dodging, but not dodging. With the 2.5D top down perspective, the slide animation just does not look or feel like a dodge, and I really think a lunge=>roll with just some sort of mini feedback (such as a sound queue) when the character lands the lunge into a roll would've been way better. But this isn't my game so whatever.

The guns do not feel good to shoot. Someone else says the gun feedback just doesn't have the OOMPH that it needs when shooting at an enemy or landing a shot on an enemy, and I agree. But also from a mechanical POV, the aiming just feels off. There's something about it that just doesn't feel good. I tried increasing my mouse speed, decreasing it, and no it didn't fix that weird feeling I get when aiming. It just felt really really off.

Finally the finishing moves is just weird. This game felt like a 2.5D bullet hell type of thing, yet there's finishers added in that just slow down the pacing altogether. You go from running and dodging bullets, avoiding melee hits, avoiding aoe, etc. (almost like Enter the Gungeon in a way) to a quick speed bump of committing a finisher (not mentioning the other minor speedup of the reloading mechanic). And that's not to mention that the finisher move is also missing that OOMPH.

Man, this is... well, mediocre. Functional, and that's about it. And I doubt it'll get better past the first hour. Maybe with like a dozen updates. EDIT 2025/06/27: Yep. Still anemic. Hard pass.

While it looks like a mix of Synthetik and Ruiner "at home", combat is anything but "brutal" and is only marginally "fast-paced". In reality it's mushy, weightless and lacking in any kind of meaningful feedback. Sounds in particular are just all-around terrible. Nothing about the encounters is exciting or fun.

Loot game... is loot game, you either like comparing numbers, or don't. Same goes for mission structure - I commend it for actually having a story progression and not being a rogue-anything, but it's nevertheless as milquetoast as it can possibly get in this day and age.

Got a consistent art direction at least, but that direction is the usual low-poly neon-y rainy cyberpunk slop that became fashionable around CP2077's pre-release hype cycle. And not even good kind of slop, like Deadlink, it's just meh, even art is just another shade of "seen that before", but there is a silver lining - it's bad enough you can actually tell it's not AI-made, so props for that. Same goes for the pre-requsite electronic music, which exists, and is 'was-there-even-music?" kind of dull.

I'm not even actively disappointed. It's just... whatever.

review:
This is literally [b]Midnight Fight Express[/b], but with loot and the ability to play with friends.
There are too many bugs at the time of EA, especially in the [u]network code[/u] when playing in coop.
[b]6 hours[/b] in coop and you finish the main story + all sub-missions at Hardcore level.
[hr][/hr]

[h1]Main cons:[/h1]
[h2]1) Loot system is broken[/h2]
The game is built on loot, from which you create your own build. On paper: the game has a bunch of stats that roll in the items you find. In fact: the builds are tied to two aspects - [u]survivability[/u] and [u]speed[/u]. There are also separate “cards” that are modifiers/gems which you put in items to get additional bonuses (such as crit, quick reload, more accuracy, etc.)
There are 4 levels of items: [b]white[/b], [b]green[/b], [b]blue [/b]and [b]red[/b].
White/Green items drop by hundreds during the mission (for each mission you get 15-20 white-green items).
Blue item you find with a smaller chance ([strike]something like 1 blue item per 2 missions[/strike]).
Red items are ultra-rare legendaries that you drop from bosses.
What you end up with: you run a level in white/green items without any “cards” (gems/modifiers) at the end of the level, you get a blue/red item of your level (because the current mission level is equal to your equipment), you put on this “super-mega-rare” red item with a lot of bonuses/perks for the next mission and at the end of this next mission (~20 minutes of real time) you get 100 white/green items [b]with stats better than you red item[/b]. [spoiler]What are these red items for then?[/spoiler]
You cannot modify/increase level, class of an item. You can only insert "cards"(gems) into a white/green/blue item and that's if you find those "cards" too. The red item can not be changed in any way, it drops with constant large number of "cards"/"perks".

[h2]2) Worthless currency[/h2]
In the game there are 2 types of currency: 
1) first to buy items(weapon/armor)
2) second to insert "cards"(gems) in the item. 
During the mission, you get a bunch of currency + as I wrote above, you receive 100 items of white-green level. After the mission, you sell 100 of white/green items for 10000 of currency and you end up with a million currency. 
Now, you have to spend this currency, but game shop is just "empty". Inside shop you can only buy white/green item(armor and weapon) with exactly the same level as you. Let me remind you that you just received 30 of the exact same items from the previous mission for free.
In 6 hours, i never bought a single item from the shop, since same items you find during the mission [u]for free[/u] and [u]with higher stats[/u].

review:
Masterpiece. 

When you play this you might find a handful of small changes you wish the game had. Perhaps dialogue options, maybe a little diversity in vehicles, or better jumping. But then, inevitably, you'll remember this is over twenty years old. The fact its this playable, this immersive, this clean that it beats blockbuster games being released right now? Amazing. It still fits like a glove. Somehow the dystopian feel, the devastated cityscapes and filthy sewage feels both classic and futuristic. The graphics may not be crystal clear, but they make a kind of grimy sense for the story. The weapons, the driving, the opponent strategy? It feels fresh. Any weakness it has in mechanics is more like a challenger to the player to do better than a valid critique of the game.

There are thrills in the combat of this game and twists in the story that are beyond many films. It's not just 'classic' in the sense of doing what many games do and having done it first... it's classic because it does it with such insane elegance. It feels definitive. Like any other alien invasion and corporate corruption story line is just a poor imitation of the Orange Box. 

Don't just play the main game, go through the episodes too. They add so much to the lore and I would say one of the side missions in Episode 2 is one of the most challenging and fulfilling combat scenarios in any game I've ever played. 

Hey, g-man, let's talk about the future and the past. I'd like some closure to the ending of Episode 2 and to keep using my skills. Count me in as one of the many, many fans who would love a Half Life 3 or Borealis franchise.

name: Arma 3
review:
This game is a military simulation game. However, it would be a mistake to evaluate it as a typical "FPS" title; it should rather be seen as a military training tool or a professional simulation platform. On the game's massive maps, planning, navigation, coordination, and communication skills are of utmost importance. Missions are often carried out not with preset strategies, but through tactical decisions made on the spot. This means the game demands not just reflexes from the player, but also leadership, teamwork, and operational thinking skills. Arma 3 is definitely not a game to be played solo; it reveals its true potential when played within organized communities, under specific rules and defined roles.
Personally, I tried the game solo for about two hours, and during that time I couldn’t establish any real coordination or take advantage of the depth the game offers. That’s because ARMA 3 requires well-thought-out operational planning and solid teamwork. Experiencing this in randomly joined public servers is nearly impossible. The learning curve is quite steep. The controls are complex, and the interface is unconventional. Getting used to this structure takes time—but this difficulty is one of the key elements that reinforces the game’s realism and professionalism. In conclusion, Arma 3 offers a serious military simulation experience that requires patience, discipline, and strategic thinking. It’s a unique platform for those who enjoy planning and execution more than casual fun.

review:
Unexpectedly good story.

After years of collecting virtual dust in my Steam library, I thought: maybe my PC can run it now.

I bought the game back when online mods like DayZ were popular. Back then, it didn't run that well on my PC. But now, after all this time and with a new PC, I decided to fire it up.

So, I never really played it and to get started I got in to story mode. At first I was confused by the controls, but after I got used to it, I was completely sucked into the story. It was exciting and immersive, I really wanted to finish it out of curiosity for what would happen next. Some bits even stuck so well that it triggered a thrill reaction when I heard certain sounds in real life. 

At some points I was a little confused what to do since most games treat the player like a toddler, here, they just leave it up to you to be creative and figure out how to solve certain problems (which I very much like).

I would definitely recommend it if you like immersion and good storytelling.

Came to build a cabin. Accidentally married a 3-legged mutant. 10/10.

Started out strong: crashed a helicopter, ate some berries (they were not safe), and befriended a silent dude named Kelvin who can't hear but can definitely feel disappointment.

Built a house. Cannibals stole it. Built another house. Accidentally set it on fire with my own torch.

Virginia (the aforementioned 3-legged ballerina sniper) now lives with me. She brought me a squirrel once. I cried.

Game teaches you survival, resourcefulness, and how fast you can scream when a cave demon crabwalks at you with zero warning.

Pros:

Kelvin will do literally anything you tell him. Except stay alive.

Base building is fun until nature revolts.

Cannibal fashion is ahead of its time.

Cons:
– Why does everything make creepy noises?
– Ate a leg once. Not proud of it.

Final verdict: If you liked camping but wished it had more mutants and existential dread—this is the game for you.

name: Sons Of The Forest
review:
Why do the basic starting enemies one shot kill you at the start of the game if you play on hard? It's incredibly boring.

I played the first one. Loved the first one. Discovering the story was great, it was a great horror game. In the original game, you spend so much time trying to survive, that when you die for the first time, and are abducted by the cannibals, it's huge, it feels like such a twist, and such an elevation of the stakes.

This game absolutely shits all over that.

So, first things first, the intro is ass. Being a soldier looking for other soldiers takes away from the personal motivation of the protagonist, and it also makes surviving not seem a problem. 

Ok, whatever. We get an NPC, Kelvin. He technically takes orders, but he mostly just does jobs badly, and he is often nowhere to be seen when enemies show up.

The enemies have been massively messed up from the original. In the original, upgrading your weapons and getting better at fighting the enemies, knowing that seeing them stalking you meant an attack, which would interrupt you, that was tense, and rewarding.

Here I have been 1 shot killed every single time. It is not tense or difficult. It's frustrating, and boring. It throws you straight to a respawn-which is a terrible imitation of the mechanic in the original where you could be abducted, and after if you died, that was it. Now, infinite respawns for infinite boredom. I ran my game as a server in case any friends wanted to join later. I played on Hard because I was assuming the game would be balanced intelligently. No, the enemies will literally one shot you if you have only the health that you start with, so you need to pound meds, or work out how to craft them. Good thing it keeps respawning you, because a single miss, or if you take damage through a couple of blocks, and you will respawn. At that point, why am I even building defenses?

I lost my patience with the AI at this point. I was finishing my base, Kelvin was putting pieces together. I jump into my inventory to craft some arrows. Despite my soldier buddy standing right next to me, a random cannibal runs up and kills me in a single shot, forcing yet another reload. I am so annoyed at this point, that I execute NPC Kelvin for gross incompetence. All I have done at this point is chop down trees, get one shot by enemies, and get annoyed at how poor the AI is.

I thought the level design was really cool at first. My instinct was to follow the river to the coast and set up there, where I'd have some clear space, and move inland. First problem: bunch of these rivers just... stop. They don't go anywhere. Ok, whatever, keep going downhill, make the coast. Oh, cool, a mutant lady. She's wearing something weird. I'll kill her before she summons more help. Oops, that's an important NPC, shouldn't have done that. Even though she resembles the multi-limbed late game enemies of the last game.

But ok, from the coast I can see two points of interest. There's a life raft in the water, and a smoke plume on a bluff nearby. That's cool! From most locations you can see a couple more interesting locations.

So I swim out to the life raft. I am immediately given a gun. I have been playing for like 20 minutes, and I have a handgun, a taser, and a metal axe. That axe was a serious upgrade in the first game, the handgun is ridiculous, why is that there, I find grenades, I have a taser. This is not progression. 

The first game made me feel I had to build a base to survive long enough to get strong enough to fight my way off the island and discover it's mystery. This game makes me feel like I'm wasting my time building something, and that the only reason to do so is to get fresh water and meds. I would not be suprised if there are speedruns where people bypass most of the building entirely.

I really did want to like this game. Feels like a lot of this wasn't even playtested-the difficulty is terrible, the enemies are not aggressive and difficult, they just hit like a truck. It doesn't feel like I'm being beaten by a hard game, like a souls game, it feels like the code is straight up wrong because who in their right mind would make such boring, dumb, enemies, hit so hard. It is not punishing you for failing at combat, it is punishing you for not farming the same health items over and over. I've put in 4 hours so far. I'm going to have to restart, on normal, and not murder the mutant, so I have both companions, and can actually explore the story, to get through.

EDIT: The one good thing I can say about this game, is that they refunded it even though I was at 4 hours in. It doesn't make my review positive, but credit to the dev/publishing team, they refunded the game fully just because I thought it was ass. It doesn't change my opinion, this game is ass and you should just play the original, which is a survival and horror CLASSIC, but the guys who made it are good lads, and I'm willing to forgive them this massive misstep and I'll be keen to see if they can improve on it in future. Massive ups boys, you made a bad game, but you have serious integrity. 

Don't buy Sons of the Forest. Don't let this game be your introduction to this story and concept. Buy the Forest, and find a mate or two to play it with. I promise, it is a great use of survival-lite ideas in a horror story.

review:
This review is written by somebody who has some history playing old-school Diablo games, and got heavily disappointed by Diablo 3 and particularly the recent Diablo 4 due to a switch in Blizzard to monetize more their game. Never really played POE or POE2 so please take my review with a grain of salt.

This game is a lot on sale, and I’ve bought it with all its extensions. Let’s put it simply: I have developed one character, finished most of the quests of all the extensions with ONE character currently at LV70, now on a playing on Elite to get it slowly, learning my build and how I want to play without looking at guides online. Reaching this point has taken 50 hours of game time, and there are dozens of ways to design a character with the new extensions.

And the verdict is I’m feeling that I’m barely scratching the surface of what can be done in terms of builds with character double classes, devotions and items. This game has no micro transaction, can be played offline not requiring a permanent online connection, on local network with others, online with others, has nice graphics, runs flawlessly on the Steam deck (use community Proton to avoid FPS stuttering due to what seems like a sound queue issue), and so on. The devs LISTEN to the community, support mods, and TAKE the time to deliver a top notch experience. You pay for the game once, and just play it. 

Do I recommend this game? Yes. Grab it. You can relax playing, thinking about how you want to play it, or just stress more and take a challenge. This game is a fresher and you will have a blast. Worth every penny.

review:
world and story are more engaging than expected. lots of secrets and sidequests but the game doesn't feel convoluted. i haven't even fully completed all of the content in the game on one character yet, but i've been figuring things out as i go and enjoying the process. i picked up on it late, but this game is really pretty exceptional, and there are a lot of qualities that put it above other known titans of the genre imo. don't sleep on it like i did; its worth the time if you have it to give. at full price its a deal, on sale it's a steal even with the expansions. visual art is dated ofc, but still compelling, and definitely nostalgic. music and atmosphere are solid, though consistently dark.

i bought the base game on sale, and expansions when i reached the cap of 85 (increases to 100 with expansions). i didn't really feel like i missed out not having the content earlier, but it definitely adds some fun gameplay loops to cycle through and push higher until you fall over. doesn't emphasize teleporting across the map and oneshotting hordes of gods as much as the competition, but the power scaling has felt consistently rewarding just making up a build as i go along (sans guides). i think i'd recommend playing through and figuring stuff out yourself, because there is a good deal of hidden stuff and making a build isn't very obtuse (though there are a lot of options), but do whatever you want. should probably get the game if you read allat tho

review:
An absolutely top tier ARPG with high replayability, with 36 possible combinations of classes, you won't be out of things to try for a good while! While some of them are more underwhelming compared to others, they are all still very viable and have their shares of items. The environment and level design are top notch, with each new area looking better than the last, merging into one beautiful world.

Speaking of the design, this game's setting does really well at blending it all together, the dark fantasy and Lovecraftian horror go together great with the whole Victorian-era vibe. The soundtrack is great as well, adding hype at points it's meant to while also able to spook you at other points.

My only gripe is that the game could definitely use a more refined loot filter system, but that's fixed easily thanks to the vast amount of mods for the game, including Rainbow Filter, which I can't recommend enough if you're really getting into the nitty gritty of your build and want to really maximize your mastery with items.

All in all, a love letter to the ARPG community that deserves all it has and more. Grab some friends or play solo, whichever one you choose, you're going to have a lot of fun. Can't wait for Fangs of Asterkarn :).

name: Grim Dawn
review:
Grim Dawn feels a lot like playing Diablo 2, which is probably my favorite action RPG of all time. It's got its own vibe and several improvements that I appreciate, like being able to use town portals (which the game calls rifts) without the need for scrolls, but rather as a skill. In Diablo 2, you had to buy more town portal scrolls once in a while and dedicate a part of your inventory (even if it was small) to a tome where you kept your town portal scrolls. I also like that your inventory got larger early on after you helped out an NPC in your main base and that there's a button to rearrange it so that more items can fit into it. 

Smashing enemies or shooting them (either with a crossbow or rifle) feels good and the skills of my Demolitionist class seem useful and varied, but I rely almost entirely on Blackwater Cocktail, which coats an area with fire for a while, so that both enemies caught in the initial blaze and those running into it after a few seconds suffer fire damage. It's great for crowd control, which is essential here, because you often run into enemy groups that come chasing after you.  

However, I'm writing this review after only 11 hours to say that I feel finished with this game. There is nothing particularly wrong or bad about it, I just don't see why I should play it anymore. I don't care about getting new skills, since Blackwater Cocktail takes care of every enemy quickly except bosses and there it's just a matter of doing it several times, along with some melee attacks if I feel like it. The lore and notes you can find are relatively interesting, I like helping out the NPCs, exploring more of the map, going into caves and all that jazz, but that's not enough to keep me playing, there's nothing that I look forward to experience. I could play more and have a good time, but I could just as well play another game. 

The fact that I've got lots of other games waiting for me and perhaps an unfair, unconscious and inevitable comparison with how it felt to play Diablo 2 all those years ago probably plays a part in my decision to uninstall Grim Dawn. I've changed over the years and become more critical, more impatient. I don't have as much time to waste as I used to and even when I do (just started my vacation) I don't want to spend that time thinking "why should I continue doing this?". Once I start to ask myself that question it's often time to move on, to see if the next game is better at holding my interest.

I thought I would enjoy Grim Dawn much more and the fact that I've written the above means that I probably won't play another action RPG for a long time. I had already put off this genre for many years (last played Victor Vran Sep 2016 according to Steam and it was okay), because while some do stuff here and there that's better than Diablo 2, the overall experience felt lacking and far from as fun as Diablo 2.

For people that like action RPGs, Grim Dawn is probably one of the best ones, much better than any I've played since Diablo 2, but for me the quest of further decreasing my backlog is far more enticing than anything Grim Dawn has to offer.

Played this game for around 200 hours on "other platforms" before I bought it on sale.

Grim dawn is undoubtedly the best ARPG game ever created. Diablo, POE do not even come close to comparing to what Grim Dawn offers in terms of progression, itemization, build variety, and the incredible story and art direction. 

The endgame is somewhat lacking compared to the other ARPGs on the market but Grim Dawn makes up for this by having the most enjoyable alt-aholic experience. 

This game encourages you to start new characters and create builds using legendary items you farm using your "main" character. The story and gameplay is very engaging and repeated playthroughs stay fresh, never feeling tedious. 

Grim Dawn has incredible depth to all of its systems and mechanics, and this can make new players feel overwhelmed. But I promise you, if you push past the early game confusion and take some time to learn and understand the mechanics, Grim Dawn is one of those games that will stick with you for a lifetime.

10/10. Buy the game. Go visit the Crate Entertainment forums to explore builds. Get decision paralysis and settle on Primal Strike Warder anyway.

review:
Grim Dawn by Crate Entertainment is a dark, atmospheric action RPG that stands as a powerful tribute to classic hack-and-slash games while carving out its own identity with deep customization and a grim, immersive world. Set in a post-apocalyptic fantasy realm ravaged by war between otherworldly forces, the game excels in delivering a richly textured narrative alongside satisfying combat mechanics and a wealth of character-building options.

One of the game’s greatest strengths is its dual-class system, which allows players to combine two distinct mastery classes from a diverse roster, resulting in highly customizable builds tailored to a variety of playstyles. Whether you prefer brutal melee combat, cunning spellcasting, or a hybrid approach, Grim Dawn rewards experimentation. The skill trees are expansive and flexible, and alongside a vast array of weapons, armor, and relics, they offer a depth of progression that keeps gameplay fresh over dozens of hours.

The world of Grim Dawn is beautifully bleak, filled with haunting landscapes, dilapidated towns, and twisted creatures that embody the game’s dark tone. The lore is thoughtfully crafted and gradually unveiled through quests, environmental storytelling, and NPC interactions, making exploration feel meaningful rather than just a backdrop for combat. The game’s atmosphere is enhanced by moody visuals and a haunting soundtrack that perfectly complement the grim setting.

Combat is engaging and tactical, balancing fast-paced action with strategic use of abilities, positioning, and resource management. Enemies come in a variety of types with unique behaviors and resistances, requiring players to adapt and optimize their gear and skills. Additionally, Grim Dawn offers multiplayer co-op and an endgame with challenging boss fights and dungeons, providing plenty of content for those who want to push their characters further.

In summary, Grim Dawn is a meticulously crafted ARPG that combines depth, atmosphere, and rewarding gameplay into an unforgettable experience. It may appeal most to fans of the genre looking for a complex character progression system and a dark fantasy world full of mystery and danger. With its engaging combat, rich customization, and evocative world, Grim Dawn remains a standout title in the action RPG landscape.

Rating: 8/10

name: Cities: Skylines
review:
[h1]🏙️ Cities: Skylines – Review[/h1]

[b]Cities: Skylines[/b] is the SimCity sequel we never officially got—but it turned out better anyway. Developed by Colossal Order, this game isn’t just about building cities—it’s about [i]mastering systems[/i], understanding flow, and praying your traffic doesn’t turn into a dystopian nightmare at rush hour.

Released in 2015 and still going strong (with a sequel now out), it remains a landmark in the city-building genre.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Strengths[/h2]

[list]
[*][b]Deep and flexible simulation[/b] – Zoning, electricity, water, sewage, education, health care, public transport, pollution—every system feels distinct and connected. You’re not just painting roads, you’re managing a living, breathing organism.

[*][b]User-friendly design tools[/b] – Road tools, snapping, curved paths, elevation controls—it’s all buttery smooth and satisfying. You can build efficient grids or artistic chaos, and both feel great.

[*][b]Massive modding support[/b] – Steam Workshop integration turned this game into an endless sandbox. Want Tokyo traffic lights? German-style police cars? A working airport system? Done. The community has added thousands of assets, mechanics, and UI improvements.

[*][b]Stunning time-lapse potential[/b] – Zoom out at night with the lights on and traffic flowing? It's [i]city-building ASMR[/i]. And it runs well on most systems—at least before you install 300 mods.

[*][b]DLC adds meaningful complexity[/b] – Unlike many live-service games, the expansions here often introduce significant gameplay elements (e.g., Green Cities, Mass Transit, Industries, Airports). It’s more than just cosmetic fluff.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Weaknesses[/h2]

[list]
[*][b]Traffic is both a feature and a curse[/b] – The traffic system is excellent… until it isn’t. One bad intersection or misplaced roundabout and your city becomes a frozen gridlock. Some players spend more time solving traffic than building cities.

[*][b]Steep learning curve for efficiency[/b] – You can make a city that [i]looks[/i] nice quickly. Making one that [b]functions[/b] well? That takes hours of tutorials and painful trial-and-error.

[*][b]Heavy reliance on mods[/b] – The vanilla game is great, but the modded experience is so much better it’s hard to go back. That also means console players get the short end of the stick.

[*][b]DLC bloat and pricing[/b] – The base game is affordable, but the full experience with all DLCs can get expensive. And some systems (like toll roads or tram networks) really should’ve been in the base game.
[/list]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Overall Impression[/h2]

[b]Cities: Skylines[/b] is a city-builder lover’s dream. It lets you be both the architect and the micromanager, the mayor and the civil engineer. It’s relaxing and stressful in equal measure—but always deeply satisfying when it all comes together.

Whether you’re creating a brutalist Soviet grid or a sprawling Californian utopia, the game gives you the tools to [i]make it real[/i]—and then challenges you to keep it alive.

[hr][/hr]

[h3]Score: [b]9.0 / 10[/b][/h3]

A modern classic in the city-building genre. [i]Cities: Skylines[/i] delivers depth, beauty, and creativity—with just enough traffic-based suffering to keep things interesting.

name: Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord
review:
It's a good game, and it's very fun. The start of the game can be very rough, so here are a few tips for getting past it and getting a stable source of income, if you know how to fight. 
Tip 1:
As soon as you start the game, choose any faction you want to be. This will not effect being able to recruit other troops from other factions. I chose Sturgia, because I wanted to build a massive army without having to pay alot of money in terms of wages.
Tip 2: In the character creation menu, after finishing the appearance of your character, choose the corresponding traits for whatever style of fighting or gameplay you want, for example, if you wanted to be an archer, choose the family of hunters etc.
Tip 3: 
PLAY THE TUTORIAL. The tutorial helps you to understand the basics of combat and combat on horseback.
Tip 4: The first thing I did whenever I loaded into my save was to go to a settlement and recruit alot of troops. I recruited the max amount I was able to (level up your clan tier to gain the ability to recruit more troops) after I did that, I went around and fought looters and sold their stuff. I also did quests. Try to avoid quests that ask for weapons or recruits and things like that, If you accept those quests and dont do them after a certain amount of time, the quest will fail and your relation with the person who gave you the quest will go down, which means things like recruiting better troops from them will be more difficult, as you would have to increase your relation with them. The quest I always would've picked was the "Deliver the herd to (city name)" as these quests were easy money, as long as you had the troops to defend the herd from looters.
Tip 5: 
Fight in tournaments, because this will give you more renown so you can reach clan tier 1 and start mercenary work. Clan tier 1 also lets you recruit even more troops than before, letting you attack looters and bandits with pretty much no problem.
Tip 6: 
When or if you do start mercenary work, like I did, choose a faction that has an ongoing war, but but before doing this, PLEASE MAKE SURE YOU HAVE THE TROOPS TO BE ABLE TO FIGHT. You also need the skill of knowing when to flee, because if you join up an army for the faction you are working for, and there is a rival faction's army chasing the army you joined, they will force a fight if they catch up to you, and trust me, in a battle, one of the main things that give you an upper hand is having more troops than the opposition, so to ensure that you don't die or get captured, I recommend you flee, if the opposition has more troops. I would save before joining an army because they will wander into enemy territory, looking to raid villages and siege castles, but if you lose a siege or a battle, you will be captured and you will lose everything you have inside your inventory.
Tip 7: 
Be patient, don't force a fight with someone who has better things or more troops than you do.
Tip 8: 
There is a difference between looters, mountain bandits, sea warriors and forest bandits, as well as the bandits in Khuzait territory and Aserai territory. Each one is more armed than you may think, so plan your fights carefully and always, ALWAYS, make sure you have more troops than the enemy, because all it could take is one arrow to the noggin and your gone.
Tip 9:
Dont ragequit. Death is apart of everyone's adventure, however long or short. This game is about strategy and war, so death is expected.
Tip 10:
The most important tip of all, have fun. This is a game, it isn't real life. If death occurs, don't be annoyed, be smart and say to yourself "What mistake did I make to make me die?" if you have a problem, overcome it. If you dont have enough dinaars to buy food for your troops, go out and make some.

I hope this review helped with the learning curve that many new players have to deal with, Have Fun!

name: Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord
review:
Bannerlord is one of those games that eats time and rewires your brain. You start thinking in troop formations and settlement income spreadsheets. I love it. It’s a fantastic medieval sandbox where you can be a mercenary, a king, a war criminal, or all three by Tuesday.

I originally bought it on GOG, but ended up picking it up again on Steam, because let’s be honest, the Workshop support is essential. The modding scene is insane. From quality-of-life tweaks to complete overhauls that turn the game into a different genre entirely, there’s no shortage of ways to play. Want magic? Sci-fi? Total realism? Crusader Kings depth? You can have all of it, sometimes in the same save.

Even unmodded, the core game is solid, huge battles, fluid combat, deep political systems, and a map that always feels alive. But mods push it into legendary territory.

If you’ve ever wanted to run your own medieval dynasty, command 200 troops in real-time combat, and then get betrayed by your own vassals because you accidentally stole a cow, this is the game for you.

Endlessly replayable. Deep. Messy in the best way. Bannerlord is one of the best strategy/action hybrids out there.

name: Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord
review:
**Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord – A Deep, Ambitious Sandbox with Room to Grow**

*Rating: ★★★★☆ (4/5)*

**Overview:**
After nearly a decade of anticipation, *Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord* finally arrived, aiming to expand on the cult success of its predecessor, *Warband*. It delivers a sprawling medieval sandbox that combines large-scale tactical warfare, deep political systems, and personal progression. While the game still has a few rough edges, it largely succeeds in giving players the tools to craft their own story in the war-torn land of Calradia.

---

### **What It Gets Right:**

**1. Massive, Dynamic World:**
Calradia is alive and ever-changing. Factions rise and fall, castles are conquered, and wars erupt with or without your involvement. The game simulates a living feudal world, and the AI factions genuinely feel like they're playing the same game as you.

**2. Combat That Feels Impactful:**
Bannerlord’s hallmark is its first- and third-person melee combat. Whether charging with a lance into a line of spearmen or holding a crumbling shield wall, battles are intense and rewarding. Mounted combat especially feels satisfying and weighty.

**3. Strategic Depth:**
You're not just a warrior—you're a commander, a trader, a diplomat, or even a king. The layered systems of vassalage, clan management, marriage alliances, and kingdom building give players plenty of strategic levers to pull.

**4. Modding Support:**
Like its predecessor, Bannerlord is fertile ground for mods. The community has already added countless enhancements, total conversions, and quality-of-life improvements, greatly extending the game's replayability.

---

### **Where It Falls Short:**

**1. Shallow Diplomacy & Repetitive Quests:**
While the sandbox offers political mechanics, diplomacy often feels limited and underdeveloped. Kingdom decisions can seem arbitrary, and there’s a lack of meaningful interaction with lords or companions outside of battle or dialogue menus.

**2. Pacing and Progression:**
The early and mid-game can feel grindy. Whether you're chasing down looters for hours or waiting for your army to be strong enough to hold territory, the progression can stall, especially without mods.

**3. Technical Hiccups:**
Performance is generally solid now, but bugs and odd AI behavior still crop up. Siege AI, in particular, can be frustrating, with troops getting stuck or making tactically baffling decisions.

---

### **Verdict:**

*Mount & Blade II: Bannerlord* is a worthy successor and a unique experience that blends personal narrative with grand strategy. It’s not a polished AAA title—more like a brilliant, evolving sandbox with immense replay value for those willing to invest the time. If you're a fan of medieval warfare or emergent storytelling, Bannerlord is absolutely worth your time, especially as its modding scene and updates continue to polish the experience.

**Recommended For:**
Fans of *Total War*, *Crusader Kings*, or *Skyrim* with a love for open-ended gameplay and large-scale combat.

**Not Recommended For:**
Players looking for a tightly scripted story, flawless AI, or fast-paced progression.

name: Sid Meier's Civilization V
review:
Civilization V is a 4x strategy game by Firaxis Games. In Civilization, the player leads their civilization from the most humble of beginnings and into the future. The maps are generated procedurally. This title features a number of victory conditions that can be obtained through research, exploration, diplomacy, expansion, and more.

The game introduced hexagonal titles instead of the square ones used in previous entries and the combat system has changed by removing unit stacking and allowing cities to defend themselves through ranged attack. The maps also added computer controlled city-states that you can trade with, leverage through diplomacy, or perhaps conquer.

Whereas the base game had a number of features missing that were in previous titles, the two expansions, Gods & Kings and Brave New World, added some of these features back, as well as bringing with them new additions. It is fair to say that Civilization V isn’t truly complete without these expansions, so I recommend the Complete Edition when purchasing.

You may well have heard people state which is their favourite Civilization game and why. I do feel that Civilization titles are somewhat like Star War trilogies, you are likely to enjoy the first one you were exposed to. This is true for myself, as I prefer Civilization V to VI overall. I had originally played V some years ago and so I feel far more comfortable with it.

In short, Civilization V is more than worthy of purchase today, especially during a sale and with the Complete Edition in mind. I expect it to once again take up many hours of my time!

[h3] A classic for a reason, Civ 5 is a game every gamer should have in their library. 5/5 [/h3] 

[i] On my scale, a 5/5 game is a masterpiece. These games stay with you and invoke the strongest sense of accomplishment, mastery, and creativity. Some may change your life, while others provide a perfect gaming experience. Some of these define their genres and cast shadows everyone else dreams of escaping, while others completely transform the genre entirely or open up a whole new pathway for game development. [/i]

Civ 5 is so good, it casts a shadow over the rest of the franchise. They need to innovate to justify why you would ever buy something new instead of Civ 5, but they already created the perfect Civ game so they’re cooked. 5 > 6 > 7

Civ 5 is like playing a virtual board game, with a ton of potential complexity (but also with a certain simplicity to it). Most of the Civs play demonstrably different, although standardized strategies continue to work. Highly recommend my personal favorite settings, which involve randomizing everything including starting Civ and seeing what you have to deal with. 

Under no circumstances should anyone ever pay full price for this. Wait for one of the quarterly steam sales when it and [i] all [/i] of the DLCs go on sale for like 90% off. Buy the bundle for like $15-20 and you have a game that will give you hundreds of hours of fun alone AND with friends. 

At the same time, under no circumstances should anyone play the base game of this. It is criminal that buying this game without DLC is even an option. You either play this with all the add ons or not at all. Base Civ is so bare it is the video game equivalent of eating cardboard.

name: Trove
review:
[h1]Trove of adventures![/h1]
[i]As i'm sure everyone would say after playing this game, where should I begin?[/i]

[b]Graphics:[/b]
If I had to say, I wouldn't say top notch. The graphics is okay, they can bug you. Minecraftish style but not as bad. There is alot more animation's, alot more detail. Do not take this the wrong way. The game hasn't done wrong, it feels right in a blocky sense of way.

[b]Gameplay:[/b]
Fantastic, that's what I say. The gameplay makes up for alot within the game. You can find alot to do. The recent ingame changes are also very nice. New level caps also I noticed. I know Trove gets some nice updates and some odd ones. Either way you cut the cake, you might still get cherries ontop. What I mean is, the updates normally consists of cons n pros, depending on wether you like cherries or not, some cons to others are pros. 
I honestly can't say how much gameplay there is while describing each one. It is just too much. You'll have to read more about it if you don't already know much. Basic gameplay is both creative and adventure. You will want friends or a club world to help out. You can own your own worlds, house, pets. You can wear any decoration, infact, the loot collector and item hunting is very uniqe making you as a player want to find every piece. Each piece you collect is saved & can be overlayered on set equipment. Base game rewards, item shop, minor NPC support. Alot to keep you going. It is mostly PvE, PvP is a thing too.

[b]SoundFX:[/b]
While being blocky in a block like world, you'd expect the characters of the world to sound different. They have nailed this. Music and sounds are pretty good. I'd have to say it wasn't expected but yes, the game sounds are good. The basic attack or hit sounds however is the same old sound, some soundFX are loopy.

[b]PTW or FTP?:[/b]
This is one of the big concerns when entering a FTP game. Yes, it is FTP. 100%
The great thing about trove is how much they actually have to offer FTP. They don't charge you for club worlds or properties, they don't charge you for alot that they could or other games had or do now. The PTW options are minor but continues to support the servers. As any game, PTW has the options to speed up you're progress towards the game or simply for cosmetic styles. It is simply a choice. Do you enjoy the game? Do you feel it is under valued? Do you feel like the devs did decent work? Questions you ask yourself may lead to you spending a few bucks. But by all means, it is only optional, the choices we're in control to make. The game I'd have to say is FTP.

[u][b]Personnal notes:[/b][/u]
This isn't survival, nor is it up to the standards of graphics these days. It is something I do enjoy playing so I must recommend it. Creativity lovers will really enjoy Trove as most already have. I do suggest playing Trove, espeacially if you don't mind low end graphics with high gameplay value. [u]Be warned,[/u] it is a MMO, it is a RPG. put these two together, you got yourself a cracked egg. The game can be very addictive as any MMORPG.

Graphics:5.0
SoundFX:6.0
Funfactor:7.5
Overall:6.5

INGREDIENTS:

1 c. unsalted butter
2 c. sugar
1/2 tsp. salt
1 c. flour
1 c. cocoa powder
4 eggs
1 (13-oz.) jar Nutella
5 Ferrero Rocher candies, unwrapped and crumbled


DIRECTIONS:

1. Preheat oven to 350 degrees F.
2. Melt butter in a medium-sized saucepan over medium heat. Add sugar, stirring until combined. 3. Remove from heat and add salt, flour, and cocoa powder, stirring to combine. Whisk in eggs, stirring just until the mixture is combined into a batter. Set aside.
4. Spray an 8"-x-8" pan with cooking spray. Pour half of the batter into the pan. Spoon or lightly drizzle most of the Nutella on top of the batter, forming an even layer over the brownie batter. 5. 5. Use a spoon or silicone spatula to cover the Nutella with the remaining brownie batter. (If you pour the batter straight on top of the Nutella, it will sink into the Nutella and combine into one marbled—yet delicious—mess.)
6. Bake until the top layer of brownies has browned and set, 28 to 30 minutes. It shouldn’t jiggle when you remove it from the oven. (The toothpick test doesn’t work here, since the toothpick will hit the Nutella layer, making the brownies seem uncooked.)
7. Let cool for 15 to 20 minutes, then top with a drizzle of Nutella and crumbled Ferrero Rocher chocolates. Cut into squares and serve.

Welcome to Civilization 6, where you accidentally declare war on Gandhi, forget why you built 7 holy sites, and just wanted to play a chill game but now you’ve been locked in a 300 year grudge match over one tile of bananas.

I don’t know what I’m doing 90% of the time. I’m clicking buttons like they owe me money. I’m building wonders while barbarians are burning my capital. But damn it, I’m LEARNING. Mostly how to read, because this game comes with enough text to make ADHD cry and dissociate into a side quest.

The worst part of this game is honestly the MULTIPLAYER mode. My significant other takes seven geological eras to make her turn.
By the time it’s my move again, I have Forgotten what I was doing, lost emotional connection with my empire, lost my identity, aged, died and reincarnated as an angry cell who now wants to nuke her just to speed things up.

But do I keep playing? Yes, yes I do. Do I still want to name my religion something dumb like “Spicy Sadness”? Yes, but won't cause toxic. 

This game is so confusing, dramatic, unintentionally funny, and mildly traumatic.. just like me.

9/10 would forget my war plan and build a library instead.

review:
As someone who’s spent nearly 600 hours on Steam alone (and 2,395 more on the Nintendo Switch), I can confidently say Civilization VI is worth your time...especially if you’re new to the series.

Admittedly, I was disappointed at launch. Core gameplay felt unbalanced, and the lack of meaningful penalties for rapid expansion made the experience shallower than Civ V. But over time...and with the excellent Rise and Fall and Gathering Storm expansions...many of those early issues have been addressed. The introduction of loyalty, governors, climate systems, and diplomatic favor added depth and restored a compelling choice between wide vs. tall strategies.

While I still rank Civ V higher overall for its more refined strategic layer, Civ VI shines in its vibrant presentation, improved online stability, and robust mod support. It feels more inviting and dynamic, even if some complexity was streamlined in the process.

If you’ve never played a Civilization game before, there has never been a better place to start than Civ VI. With all the DLC in place, this is a complete, deeply engaging experience that will easily steal hundreds of hours of your life—in the best way possible.
